stages.label: Prepare and verify the parties
stages.goal: Know exactly who you are dealing with before sharing anything.
gate: Who signs the sales contract, issues the invoice and receives the LC proceeds?
Company registry, directors and beneficial owners checked
Sanctions and adverse-media screening done
ISCC and licence numbers verified in public databases
Volume plausible for the stated capacity
Chain mapped: no more than two undocumented layers
traps: Blind chains that refuse video calls
Mandates that stop before the owner

stages.label: Demand, offer and protection
stages.goal: Turn a lead into a protected, priced opportunity.
gate: Buyer demand has a price basis: benchmark, premium or discount, basis and pricing period
Seller offer names the product, spec, port, window and validity
Proof of product is verifiable, not just PDFs
Commission agreement and NCNDA signed before identities are shared
No fees requested before a verified contract

stages.label: Negotiation and contract
stages.goal: Write every duty down before anything moves.
gate: Price formula and benchmark defined
Incoterm named with its edition
Inspector, sampling and final-and-binding rule agreed
Sustainability warranties and documents included
Law, arbitration seat and change-in-law clause agreed
Brokerage arrangement stays in a separate agreement
traps: Mismatch between contract and LC terms
Naming the broker's fee where it should not appear

stages.label: Payment security
stages.goal: Make sure the money is guaranteed before the oil leaves.
gate: LC text compared line by line with the contract
Issuing bank and confirmation decided
LC opened before the loading window
Document list achievable by the seller
Banking charges allocated
Commission payment route agreed in writing
traps: Escrow proposed for a bulk cargo

stages.label: Logistics, inspection and loading
stages.goal: Ship the right cargo on a verified vessel with independent measurement.
gate: Vessel IMO, ownership and sanctions checked
Tank inspection and cleanliness confirmed
Independent inspector appointed and briefed
Sealed samples taken and retained
Quantity and quality certificates consistent

stages.label: Transit and documents
stages.goal: Move the paper as carefully as the oil.
gate: Bill of lading clean and shipped on board
Documents match the LC line by line
Sustainability proof and Union Database records in order
Export and import customs papers consistent
Plan for documents arriving after the ship
traps: Small spelling discrepancies that block payment

stages.label: Discharge, claims, payment and commission
stages.goal: Close the deal: settle claims, get paid, get your fee.
gate: Discharge inspection done
Claims noticed within contract time limits
Documents presented and bank payment received
Commission paid as agreed
Records kept for audits
traps: Records that do not match certificates

entries.title: Payment-method spectrum: who carries the risk
entries.in_plain_words: Every payment method decides who has to trust whom: the seller, the buyer or a bank.
entries.in_detail: Ranked from most seller-friendly to most buyer-friendly: cash in advance, confirmed irrevocable LC, unconfirmed irrevocable LC, documentary collection D/P, D/A, open account (optionally insured). Real deals blend methods, e.g. a down payment plus an LC. The side with more bargaining power usually imposes the method, so the method itself shows who needs the deal more.
options_and_variants: Cash in advance (T/T): Seller safest, buyer most exposed
Confirmed irrevocable LC: Two banks promise to pay
Unconfirmed irrevocable LC: One bank promises to pay
Documentary collection D/P: Banks release documents against payment, no guarantee
Documentary collection D/A: Documents released against a promise to pay later
Open account: Seller finances the buyer; needs insurance or standby
entries.for_a_broker: Your commission is only as safe as the payment method. Ask for it early.

entries.title: T/T in advance (prepayment, incl. split payment)
entries.in_plain_words: The buyer wires money before the goods ship.
entries.in_detail: Telegraphic transfer (SWIFT MT103) paid before shipment, in full or as a down payment with the balance against documents. Best for the seller, worst for the buyer. Legitimate between parties with a proven record, small lots or scarce supply. With an unverified seller it is the classic advance-fee pattern. Safer versions: refundable advance backed by an advance payment guarantee, escrow with a regulated agent, or payment against an independent inspector's certificate.
risks_and_red_flags: Total loss if the seller does not exist
Often disguised as 'registration', 'inspection' or 'bond' fees
entries.for_a_broker: Never steer a buyer into prepaying an unverified seller.
entries.verify_note: Original document called this 'never acceptable'; it is a legitimate but high-risk method.

entries.title: Cash against documents (CAD)
entries.in_plain_words: Payment is due when the seller presents the shipping documents.
entries.in_detail: A contract term, not a formal bank procedure: the buyer pays on presentation of the agreed documents (original B/L, certificates), usually via its bank. The seller keeps control of the cargo while originals are held. If the buyer refuses to pay, cargo can sit in port and generate demurrage and storage costs. Do not confuse with documentary collection D/P, which follows ICC URC 522.
risks_and_red_flags: Stranded cargo if buyer refuses
No bank payment undertaking

entries.title: Documentary collection - D/P (documents against payment)
entries.in_plain_words: Banks hand the shipping documents to the buyer only when the buyer pays.
entries.in_detail: The seller ships and sends documents to its bank (remitting bank), which forwards them to the buyer's bank (collecting/presenting bank). The buyer receives the documents, and with them the cargo, only after paying. Banks handle documents only and give no payment guarantee, so the seller carries buyer risk and stranded-cargo risk.
risks_and_red_flags: No guarantee of payment
Cargo may be refused at destination

entries.title: Documentary collection - D/A (documents against acceptance)
entries.in_plain_words: The buyer gets the documents by signing a promise to pay later.
entries.in_detail: The seller draws a time draft (bill of exchange) payable e.g. 30, 60 or 90 days after sight or B/L date. The buyer accepts it to receive the documents and the cargo, and pays at maturity. A bank can add an 'aval' (guarantee) to the draft. It is an accepted draft, not a simple promissory note. Highest non-payment risk among collection methods because the cargo is already released.
risks_and_red_flags: Cargo released before payment

entries.title: Open account
entries.in_plain_words: Goods ship first; the buyer pays later by wire.
entries.in_detail: Standard between established partners. The seller extends unsecured credit (often 30-90 days) and carries all buyer risk. Mitigations: trade credit insurance, standby L/C or bank guarantee, factoring or forfaiting, parent guarantees. Not suitable for new counterparties.
risks_and_red_flags: Unsecured exposure for the full invoice
entries.verify_note: Original called it 'commercial suicide'; accurate only without protection.

entries.title: Trade credit insurance
entries.in_plain_words: Insurance that pays the seller if the buyer does not pay.
entries.in_detail: Private insurers or export credit agencies cover commercial and political non-payment risk, normally for less than 100% of the invoice and within buyer credit limits. Disputes about quality or performance are generally excluded.
risks_and_red_flags: Policy limits and exclusions
Insurer may withdraw cover on a weakening buyer

entries.title: Documentary letter of credit (LC / DLC) - overview
entries.in_plain_words: A bank's promise to pay the seller if the seller presents exactly the documents the credit requires.
entries.in_detail: Governed by ICC UCP 600. Parties: applicant (buyer), issuing bank, advising bank, beneficiary (seller), optional confirming bank, nominated bank. Flow: sale contract, buyer applies, issuing bank issues (SWIFT MT700), advising bank advises, seller ships and presents documents, banks examine (up to 5 banking days, art. 14), then pay, accept or negotiate. Principles: independent of the sale contract (art. 4); banks deal in documents, not goods (art. 5); strict compliance; credits are irrevocable (art. 3); presentation normally within 21 calendar days after shipment and before expiry (art. 14(c)).
options_and_variants: At sight: Paid after compliant presentation
Deferred payment / usance: Paid at a later date
Acceptance credit: Bank accepts a time draft
Negotiation credit: Nominated bank buys the documents; restricted or freely negotiable
Confirmed / silent confirmation: Second bank adds its promise
Transferable: Pass to supplier(s)
Back-to-back: Second credit backed by the first
Revolving: Reinstates for repeated shipments
Red / green clause: Pre-shipment advance
Standby (SBLC): Pays only on default
risks_and_red_flags: Any discrepancy can block payment even if the oil is perfect
Issuing-bank credit risk unless confirmed
entries.for_a_broker: Check LC terms against the SPA before loading; your commission usually depends on the LC paying.

entries.title: LC at sight
entries.in_plain_words: The bank pays once it has checked that the documents comply.
entries.in_detail: Payment follows a compliant presentation. UCP 600 gives the bank up to five banking days after presentation to examine, so 'at sight' is not same-day. Payment may come from the issuing, nominated or confirming bank. On discrepancies the bank may refuse or ask the applicant for a waiver.
risks_and_red_flags: Discrepancy stops payment
entries.verify_note: Original said 'about 3-5 days after B/L'; the rule is a maximum of 5 banking days to examine.

entries.title: Deferred-payment and acceptance LC (usance)
entries.in_plain_words: The bank pays at a later date, e.g. 60 days after the B/L date.
entries.in_detail: Maturity is counted from the date stated in the credit: B/L date, presentation, acceptance or sight. Two forms: deferred payment undertaking (no draft) and acceptance credit (bank accepts a draft, which can be discounted for early cash). Gives the buyer credit time; the seller can discount at a cost. Sellers usually want such credits confirmed.
risks_and_red_flags: Discounting cost erodes margin
Weak issuing bank

entries.title: Confirmed LC (incl. silent confirmation)
entries.in_plain_words: A second bank adds its own promise to pay.
entries.in_detail: A confirming bank, usually in the seller's country, takes on the undertaking in addition to the issuing bank (UCP 600 art. 8), removing issuing-bank and country risk for the seller. The fee is negotiated and often borne by the beneficiary. 'Silent confirmation' means the seller arranges confirmation privately with a bank, without the issuing bank's involvement.

entries.title: Transferable LC
entries.in_plain_words: The seller, often a trader, can pass all or part of the credit to its supplier.
entries.in_detail: Must be expressly marked 'transferable' (UCP 600 art. 38). The first beneficiary can transfer to one or more second beneficiaries; a second beneficiary cannot request a further transfer. The trader may substitute its own invoice (and draft), keeping its margin and hiding supplier or buyer identity. The transferred credit may reduce amount, unit price, shipment period and expiry, and may increase insurance cover. Needs a bank willing to act as transferring bank.
risks_and_red_flags: Second beneficiary relies on a credit issued for someone else
Can be combined with switch bills to hide origin
entries.for_a_broker: Typical for traders without production; brokers rarely benefit directly.

entries.title: Back-to-back LC
entries.in_plain_words: Two separate credits: the second one is backed by the first.
entries.in_detail: The trader's buyer opens a master LC in the trader's favour. The trader uses it as security to have its own bank open a second LC for its supplier. The two credits are independent, so mismatches between them are a real risk. Depends on the trader's bank appetite and credit line; costs add up.
risks_and_red_flags: Mismatched terms between the two credits
Bank may refuse

entries.title: Assignment of LC proceeds
entries.in_plain_words: The seller instructs that part of the money from the LC goes to someone else.
entries.in_detail: UCP 600 art. 39: a credit that is not transferable still lets the beneficiary assign proceeds under applicable law. It covers only the money, not the right to perform under the credit. Used to pay suppliers or other parties from proceeds. The bank must acknowledge it and is not obliged to act without agreeing.
entries.for_a_broker: One way a commission payout can be tied to LC proceeds, if the bank agrees.

entries.title: Revolving LC
entries.in_plain_words: A credit that renews automatically for repeated shipments.
entries.in_detail: Reinstates its amount after each drawing (by value or by time; cumulative or non-cumulative). Fits term supply such as monthly cargoes: one facility instead of opening a new LC each month. Requires careful drafting of reinstatement conditions.
entries.for_a_broker: Relevant to a monthly programme such as 5,000 t/month.

entries.title: Red-clause and green-clause LC
entries.in_plain_words: A credit that lets the seller draw an advance before shipping.
entries.in_detail: Red clause: advance against a simple receipt or undertaking to ship. Green clause: also covers storage of goods before shipment. Used for pre-export finance. Heavy risk for the applicant if goods never ship.
risks_and_red_flags: Applicant bears advance risk

entries.title: Standby letter of credit (SBLC)
entries.in_plain_words: A bank guarantee that pays only if the buyer fails to pay.
entries.in_detail: Governed by ISP98 or, to the extent applicable, UCP 600 or URDG 758. Normally issued by SWIFT MT760. Drawn by presenting a statement of default. Backs open-account trades, financial obligations or performance. A commercial LC is the primary payment route; a standby is the fallback. Unlike a documentary LC, it is not normally the way the seller gets paid.
entries.verify_note: Original said 'only if open account is used'; standbys are also used as financial or performance guarantees.

entries.title: Demand guarantee (URDG 758)
entries.in_plain_words: A bank promise to pay on first written demand, independent of the contract.
entries.in_detail: Governed by ICC URDG 758. Types: performance guarantee, advance payment guarantee, bid/tender bond, payment guarantee, retention or warranty guarantee. Payment is triggered by a compliant demand, not by proof of default in the contract.
options_and_variants: Performance guarantee: Compensates non-delivery
Advance payment guarantee: Refund of a prepayment
Bid / tender bond: Backs a tender offer
Payment guarantee: Backs the buyer's payment
Retention / warranty: Covers post-delivery obligations

entries.title: Performance bond (PB)
entries.in_plain_words: A guarantee from the seller's bank that pays the buyer if the seller does not deliver.
entries.in_detail: Common in tenders and large supply contracts. The percentage and wording are negotiated; there is no standard percentage. In unsolicited broker-chain deals, a performance bond demanded early, or a fee demanded to obtain one from a 'provider', is a classic advance-fee pattern.
risks_and_red_flags: Fee-for-bond requests from intermediaries
entries.verify_note: Original quoted 2%-3%; that is not a market standard.

entries.title: Advance payment guarantee (APG)
entries.in_plain_words: The seller's bank guarantees to refund any advance if the seller does not deliver.
entries.in_detail: Makes a prepayment safer for the buyer. Issued under URDG 758 or similar. Should be issued by a bank the buyer can verify directly, and should reduce as delivery progresses.

entries.title: Escrow
entries.in_plain_words: A neutral party holds the money until the agreed conditions are met.
entries.in_detail: A regulated bank or law firm client account holds funds and releases them against agreed evidence such as an inspector's certificate or a B/L. For bulk cargoes it is rarely used: millions of dollars sit locked while release depends on a third party's confirmation, and a ship waiting for that release runs up demurrage that can reach tens of thousands of dollars a day. The standard instrument for bulk is the letter of credit, confirmed if needed, or a standby-backed arrangement. Escrow fits small parcels such as ISO tank or container lots, deposits, or holding a performance deposit. The agent must be independently verifiable, and conflicts of interest arise if one side chooses and pays the agent.
risks_and_red_flags: Not a bulk-cargo standard: locked funds and demurrage risk
Fake 'escrow' websites
Agent not regulated or not independent
entries.for_a_broker: If a buyer or seller proposes escrow for a full cargo, ask why not a letter of credit.
entries.verify_note: Earlier version did not stress that escrow is not a bulk-cargo standard.

entries.title: Trade-finance toolbox
entries.in_plain_words: Ways to get cash earlier or carry the working capital of a deal.
entries.in_detail: These are financing, not payment-security, instruments. They sit on top of an LC or receivable.
options_and_variants: LC discounting: Bank pays now against a deferred LC, deducts interest
Forfaiting: Non-recourse purchase of deferred payment obligations
Factoring / receivables finance: Advance against invoices
Pre-export finance: Funds production before shipment
Inventory / warehouse-receipt finance: Loans against stored goods
Supply-chain finance: Bank pays suppliers early on buyer approval
Structured commodity finance: Facility secured by goods and contracts

entries.title: Proof of funds (PoF)
entries.in_plain_words: A document showing that the buyer has the money.
entries.in_detail: Bank statement, audited accounts or a credit line letter. As a PDF it is easy to forge, so it is weak evidence. Verify by having your bank or the seller's bank contact the issuing bank through independently sourced contacts. A verifiable credit line or an LC from a first-class bank is stronger.
risks_and_red_flags: Forged or recycled statements
Funds that are not available for the deal

entries.title: Bank comfort letter (BCL) and 'ready, willing and able' (RWA) letter
entries.in_plain_words: A bank letter saying a client is able to do the deal.
entries.in_detail: Non-binding. Used for credibility, not payment. If a buyer's bank will not issue one, the substitute is audited financials, a credit report or a verifiable credit line, not a public corporate profile.
risks_and_red_flags: Letters from the buyer's own finance officer are not bank confirmations
entries.verify_note: Original suggested substituting a public corporate profile; that is not evidence of payment capacity.

entries.title: How a broker actually gets paid
entries.in_plain_words: Your fee comes from a written agreement and a bank wire, not from the sale contract itself.
entries.in_detail: Typical routes: (1) commission agreement with the seller or buyer, paid by wire after payment under the SPA; (2) payment instruction or assignment of LC proceeds, if the bank agrees; (3) a separate agreement with a payout trigger such as 'seller has received payment'; (4) roll-over clause for later shipments; (5) trading margin if you take title (then you are a trader, not a broker). A reference to the broker's fee inside the SPA does not make the bank pay it automatically.
risks_and_red_flags: Commission depends on the payer's honesty if there is no instruction to a bank
Chains where each link expects a share
entries.for_a_broker: Define payer, trigger, currency, wire route, duration and roll-overs in writing.

entries.title: Currency and price hedging
entries.in_plain_words: Protecting the deal from exchange-rate and price swings.
entries.in_detail: Traders who hold price exposure may hedge with swaps or futures on correlated products; invoices in a currency other than the payer's own create FX risk that forwards can cover. A pure broker with no title has little direct exposure, but the buyer and seller price formulas still move the deal.

entries.title: LC costs and who pays
entries.in_plain_words: Banks charge fees at every step; the contract says who pays.
entries.in_detail: Typical charges: issuance, advising, confirmation, amendment, discrepancy, negotiation or discounting. Issuance cost depends on the applicant's credit and any cash margin required. Common wording puts charges outside the issuing bank's country on the beneficiary. For the buyer, an LC also uses up credit lines or ties up cash.

entries.title: The ICC and banking rulebook
entries.in_plain_words: The set of rules banks and traders use so documents and payments work the same way everywhere.
entries.in_detail: Most trade-finance and shipping rules come from the ICC. They apply only when incorporated by reference in the contract or instrument. Market-custom papers such as NCNDA, IMFPA, ICPO, SCO and FCO are not ICC instruments.
options_and_variants: UCP 600: Documentary credits
ISBP 745: How banks examine documents under UCP 600
eUCP 2.1: Electronic presentation under UCP
URC 522: Documentary collections
URDG 758: Demand guarantees
ISP98: Standby letters of credit
URR 725: Bank-to-bank reimbursement
URF 800: Forfaiting
Incoterms 2020: Delivery terms
entries.verify_note: Check current edition numbers (e.g. eUCP) on the ICC site.

entries.title: UCP 600: key articles to know
entries.in_plain_words: The few articles that decide most LC disputes.
entries.in_detail: Art. 3 credits are irrevocable. Art. 4 the credit is independent of the sale contract. Art. 5 banks deal in documents, not goods. Art. 8 confirming bank. Art. 14 examination (max 5 banking days; presentation within 21 days of shipment). Art. 16 refusal. Art. 17 originals and copies. Art. 18 commercial invoice. Arts. 19-25 transport documents (20 bill of lading, 21 sea waybill, 22 charter-party B/L). Art. 27 clean transport document. Art. 28 insurance. Art. 30 tolerances. Art. 38 transferable. Art. 39 assignment of proceeds.

entries.title: SWIFT messages you will see
entries.in_plain_words: Banks talk to each other in numbered messages.
entries.in_detail: Documentary credits and guarantees travel as category-7 messages. A real credit is issued by the issuing bank's own SWIFT message, not by a PDF from a seller or broker.
options_and_variants: MT700: Issue of a documentary credit
MT707: Amendment to a credit
MT710: Advice of a third bank's credit
MT720: Transfer of a credit
MT734: Advice of refusal
MT742: Reimbursement claim
MT750: Advice of discrepancy
MT756: Advice of reimbursement or payment
MT760: Issue of guarantee or standby
MT767: Guarantee amendment
MT799: Free-format message
MT103: Customer credit transfer
MT202: Bank-to-bank transfer
entries.verify_note: Verify message numbers against the current SWIFT standards release.

entries.title: MT799 free-format messages
entries.in_plain_words: A bank-to-bank note with no payment obligation.
entries.in_detail: Banks use it to exchange information. It is widely abused in fraud, e.g. 'proof of funds' or 'pre-advice' messages sold by intermediaries. Genuine ones come bank to bank and create no obligation to pay.
risks_and_red_flags: Sold by intermediaries as 'proof of funds'
Any request to pay a fee for one

entries.title: Common LC discrepancies and what to do
entries.in_plain_words: Small mismatches that stop the bank paying.
entries.in_detail: Typical: late shipment or presentation, description different from the credit, missing originals or signatures, unclean B/L, wrong port, quantity outside tolerance (UCP 600 art. 30 allows +/-5% for bulk not counted in units), amount over credit, expired credit, insufficient insurance, inconsistent names or data across documents. Remedies: correct within validity, ask the applicant for a waiver via the issuing bank, or present under reserve. Banks charge discrepancy fees.
entries.for_a_broker: Ask the seller's bank to pre-check draft documents.

entries.title: Banks in an LC and what each does
entries.in_plain_words: Different banks play different roles in one credit.
entries.in_detail: Issuing bank (buyer's), advising bank (tells the seller), confirming bank (adds a promise), nominated bank (authorised to pay, accept or negotiate), negotiating bank (buys the documents), reimbursing bank (settles between banks). In collections: remitting bank (seller's) and collecting/presenting bank (buyer's).

entries.title: Enquiry / RFQ (request for quotation)
entries.in_plain_words: A buyer asks suppliers what they can offer and at what price.
entries.in_detail: States product, specification, volume, period, delivery port, certification, Incoterm and payment terms. Non-binding. A serious RFQ is complete and comes from a verifiable corporate address; a vague one with no volume or spec is a fishing exercise.
risks_and_red_flags: No volume, spec or company details
Same enquiry circulating through several brokers

entries.title: Tender / RFP
entries.in_plain_words: A formal competitive process run by a large buyer.
entries.in_detail: Has written rules, deadlines, evaluation criteria and often bid bonds. The strongest signal of real demand because it is run by the buyer's procurement function. Rules of the tender override informal exchanges.

entries.title: Letter of intent (LOI)
entries.in_plain_words: A letter saying the buyer intends to buy, without committing.
entries.in_detail: Normally non-binding, except clauses that say otherwise (confidentiality, exclusivity, costs). Binding effect depends on wording and governing law. Not to be confused with a letter of indemnity, which is also abbreviated LOI.
risks_and_red_flags: Being treated as proof of purchase

entries.title: ICPO (irrevocable corporate purchase order)
entries.in_plain_words: A buyer's statement that it will buy on the terms of an offer.
entries.in_detail: Market custom in broker chains, not defined by law. The word 'irrevocable' does not make it binding by itself; effect depends on wording and law. To be actionable for a broker it needs the product and specification, volume and delivery schedule, Incoterm and port, payment method and, above all, a target price or price formula: a named benchmark (for example Argus or another assessment) plus or minus a stated premium or discount, the basis (FOB origin or CIF destination) and the pricing period. Without a price basis the broker negotiates blind against the market. Naming the buyer in an ICPO reveals its identity, so NCNDA timing must be planned. Sequence varies: seller SCO then buyer ICPO, or buyer-led RFQ and LOI then SCO. Large corporate buyers often use their own procurement documents instead.
risks_and_red_flags: No target price or price basis
Many ICPOs, no banks, no contract
Unverifiable sender
entries.for_a_broker: Do not shop an ICPO without a price basis: ask for the benchmark, the premium or discount and the basis.
entries.verify_note: Earlier version listed price only as 'price basis'; the target price or formula is now explicit.

entries.title: SCO (soft corporate offer)
entries.in_plain_words: A first, non-committal offer from the seller.
entries.in_detail: Preliminary offer to test interest: product, indicative price, availability, loading port. Normally not binding, though wording and law decide. Often exchanged before names are disclosed.

entries.title: FCO (full corporate offer)
entries.in_plain_words: A complete, formal offer from the seller.
entries.in_detail: Names the seller, product, quantity, price formula, delivery, payment, documents and validity period. May bind the seller if accepted in time, depending on wording and governing law. Validity is negotiated; 48-72 hours is common talk but not a rule.
entries.verify_note: Original said 'binding, expires in 48/72 hours'.

entries.title: Term sheet / heads of terms / MOU
entries.in_plain_words: A short summary of the main terms before the full contract.
entries.in_detail: Agrees price mechanism, volume, quality, Incoterm, payment, inspection and law. Mostly non-binding, with some binding clauses (confidentiality, exclusivity, costs). Corporate buyers often use it as the step between KYC and the SPA.

entries.title: Proof of product (PoP)
entries.in_plain_words: Evidence that the seller really has the product.
entries.in_detail: Umbrella term for papers claiming a product exists and is available. Strength ranges widely, and PoP is not proof of title.
options_and_variants: Soft PoP (copies, PDFs, videos): Weakest; easy to forge
Spec sheet and COA: Medium; depends on lab and lot link
ISCC certificate verified in public database: Strong for status, not for volume
Inspector reports from earlier shipments: Medium to strong if verifiable
Tank storage receipt confirmed by terminal: Strong
Site visit plus independent sampling: Strongest
risks_and_red_flags: Refusal to allow any independent verification
Pay-to-see-sample demands
entries.verify_note: Original said refusal of SGS pre-inspection means no product; it is a strong warning sign, not proof.

entries.title: Tank storage receipt (TSR)
entries.in_plain_words: A terminal's receipt saying a named tank holds the product for a named party.
entries.in_detail: Issued by the terminal operator and best verified by contacting the terminal directly through independently found details. Shows existence and custody, not necessarily ownership or quality.
risks_and_red_flags: Receipt not confirmed by the terminal

entries.title: Allocation / availability letter
entries.in_plain_words: A producer or refinery saying it will make volume available.
entries.in_detail: Shows a supply route, not delivered product. Check who signed, whether the signer has authority and whether the producer is certified for the stated product.

entries.title: Mandate / letter of authority (LOA)
entries.in_plain_words: Written permission from a principal to act for it.
entries.in_detail: Names who authorises whom, for which product, volume, price or price mechanism, validity, commission, exclusivity and whether sub-mandating is allowed. Verify with the issuer through independent contact details. Seller-side: 'authority to sell'. Buyer-side: 'authority to buy'. A broker working directly with a company's employees may not need one but should verify others' mandates.

entries.title: NDA
entries.in_plain_words: A promise to keep information secret.
entries.in_detail: Confidentiality only. It does not stop someone from bypassing you.

entries.title: NCNDA (non-circumvention, non-disclosure and working agreement)
entries.in_plain_words: A promise not to bypass you and not to leak names.
entries.in_detail: Market custom, not an ICC instrument. Key terms: parties including affiliates and beneficial owners, protected contacts and deals, duration, treatment of roll-overs, penalties or fee on circumvention, governing law and arbitration. It prohibits bypassing but does not by itself create a right to be paid; that comes from a commission agreement. Hard to enforce across borders, and many large companies will not sign third-party NCNDAs. Templates are cheap and often copy meaningless references.
risks_and_red_flags: Template with references to 'ICC 400/500/600'
Parties defined without affiliates
entries.verify_note: Original called it 'an ICC contract'; it is not.

entries.title: IMFPA (irrevocable master fee protection agreement)
entries.in_plain_words: A document fixing the broker's fee and how it is protected.
entries.in_detail: Market custom, normally signed with or after the NCNDA. Defines the fee (per ton or percentage), payer, trigger, payment route and roll-overs. It is a private contract, not a bank payment order. Payment depends on a separate instruction or the payer's wire. Often conditioned on buyer and seller actually closing their contract.
entries.verify_note: Original said it 'becomes a bank payment order'.

entries.title: Commission / fee agreement (direct)
entries.in_plain_words: A contract between you and whoever pays you.
entries.in_detail: The most solid protection. Checklist: 1) parties including affiliates; 2) scope (product, buyer, seller, period); 3) commission (per ton or percentage) and base; 4) payout trigger (e.g. seller has received payment); 5) payer, timing and wire route; 6) duration and roll-overs; 7) governing law and arbitration; 8) names and splits of sub-brokers. Check whether commercial-agent law applies (see comp-commercial-agent-law).

entries.title: Commission-split / joint-working agreement between brokers
entries.in_plain_words: An agreement on how brokers in a chain share one fee.
entries.in_detail: Names every broker, their share, who pays whom and what happens if the chain changes. Without it you depend on the goodwill of people you may never meet.

entries.title: Letter of introduction
entries.in_plain_words: A letter presenting you to a party.
entries.in_detail: Weak by itself. Better as an email from the buyer's corporate domain, or a three-way call confirming your role.

entries.title: KYC / company information pack (CIS)
entries.in_plain_words: The set of documents each party gives so the other can check who it is.
entries.in_detail: Typical content: certificate of incorporation, registry extract, articles, shareholder register and UBO declaration, directors' IDs, board resolution and specimen signatures, bank reference, audited accounts, licences (ISCC certificate, MPOB licence, waste or collection licences), sanctions declaration, compliance questionnaire. Passport copies and personal data are regulated; exchange them securely.

entries.title: Ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) declaration
entries.in_plain_words: A statement of the real people who own or control the company.
entries.in_detail: Reveals related entities used to bypass a broker (a 'second company' owned by the same group) and sanction exposure. Cross-check against registers where available.

entries.title: Sanitised (anonymised) COA
entries.in_plain_words: A lab analysis with names removed for a first technical screen.
entries.in_detail: Acceptable for screening only, because with the lab and supplier removed it cannot be verified. Replace it with a full COA tied to a specific tank or lot, ideally from an independent laboratory and supported by inspector sampling.
risks_and_red_flags: Cannot be traced to a lab or lot
entries.verify_note: Example specs in the original (e.g. M&I 4%) are illustrative; every buyer has its own spec.

entries.title: Specification sheet
entries.in_plain_words: The seller's description of its product's typical quality.
entries.in_detail: Lists parameters such as FFA, moisture and impurities, and others. Not a guarantee; the contract specification and penalties are what count.

entries.title: ISCC certificate (and how to verify it)
entries.in_plain_words: The sustainability certificate of a company in the supply chain.
entries.in_detail: Shows certificate number, scope (e.g. collecting point, trader, trader with storage, processing unit), products, sites, certification body and validity (one year, audited annually). Verify in ISCC's public database and match legal name and sites to the counterparty. A certificate does not guarantee volume or that a specific lot is compliant.

entries.title: Seller / buyer 'procedure' document
entries.in_plain_words: A step-by-step process one side sends to the other.
entries.in_detail: Common in broker chains. Fine if it describes steps in order. A warning sign if it asks for fees, bonds or deposits before a verified contract and verified counterparties.
risks_and_red_flags: Fees or bonds requested before contract

entries.title: Price indication
entries.in_plain_words: An order-of-magnitude price without commitment.
entries.in_detail: Often quoted as a premium or discount to a benchmark. Not an offer. A price far below any published benchmark is a warning sign, not an opportunity.

entries.title: SPA - Sale and Purchase Agreement
entries.in_plain_words: The contract in which one party sells and the other buys the goods.
entries.in_detail: In commodity trading SPA means Sale and Purchase Agreement. It fixes product, quantity, price, delivery, payment, inspection, documents, risk, sustainability duties, law and disputes. It is the first paper that truly commits both sides, backed by the LC. Either party may draft it; corporate buyers often use their own paper and sector forms may be incorporated.

entries.title: Share Purchase Agreement (not the same SPA)
entries.in_plain_words: A contract to buy shares of a company, not goods.
entries.in_detail: Used in mergers and acquisitions. Shares the acronym SPA with the commodity sale contract. Do not mix them: a goods contract moves oil, a share purchase moves ownership of a company.

entries.title: SPA variants
entries.in_plain_words: The same contract in different shapes.
entries.in_detail: The shape depends on whether the deal is one cargo or a programme.
options_and_variants: Spot: One cargo, one contract
Term / framework with call-offs: Master contract for the year; monthly nominations as call-offs
Evergreen: Rolls over until terminated
Tender-based: Result of a formal tender
Back-to-back: Trader sells and buys on matching terms
String contract: One of several sales of the same cargo down a chain
entries.for_a_broker: A 5,000 t/month requirement points to a term or framework structure.

entries.title: Sale confirmation / recap
entries.in_plain_words: A short document confirming a trade made on standard terms.
entries.in_detail: Lists the commercial points (product, quantity, price, delivery, payment) and refers to a standard contract form or general terms for the rest.

entries.title: General terms and sector standard forms (e.g. FOSFA)
entries.in_plain_words: Ready-made contract terms from trade bodies.
entries.in_detail: FOSFA International publishes standard contract forms and arbitration rules for oils and fats. Incorporating them brings a full set of rules by reference. Battle of the forms: when each party refers to its own general terms, the result can be unclear unless the contract says which prevail.
entries.verify_note: Confirm which FOSFA forms fit UCO and POME and whether the counterparty uses them.

entries.title: Incoterms 2020 - all eleven rules
entries.in_plain_words: Standard abbreviations that say who does what and where risk passes.
entries.in_detail: Published by the ICC; apply only if named in the contract, with the Incoterms 2020 edition stated. FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are for sea and inland waterway; the others suit any mode.
options_and_variants: EXW: Ex works: buyer collects at seller's premises
FCA: Free carrier: seller hands over to carrier at named place
CPT: Carriage paid to
CIP: Carriage and insurance paid to (insurance minimum clause A)
DAP: Delivered at place
DPU: Delivered at place unloaded
DDP: Delivered duty paid
FAS: Free alongside ship
FOB: Free on board
CFR: Cost and freight
CIF: Cost, insurance and freight (insurance minimum clause C)
entries.verify_note: Check that no newer Incoterms edition has been published.

entries.title: FOB (free on board)
entries.in_plain_words: The seller loads the goods on the buyer's ship; after that the buyer carries the risk.
entries.in_detail: Seller delivers when goods are on board the vessel the buyer nominates at the named loading port, and clears export. Buyer pays freight and insurance and carries risk from loading. Buyer nominates the vessel and sends notices; seller wants the LC before accepting the vessel and loading.
risks_and_red_flags: Vessel nomination failures
Demurrage disputes

entries.title: CIF (cost, insurance and freight)
entries.in_plain_words: The seller pays transport and insurance to the destination port, but the risk passes at loading.
entries.in_detail: Seller contracts and pays carriage and insurance to the named destination port. Risk passes to the buyer when goods are on board at the loading port, even though the seller pays freight. Minimum insurance under Incoterms 2020 is Institute Cargo Clauses (C), at 110% of price; parties may agree higher cover. Documents include the insurance certificate.
entries.verify_note: Original said Institute Clauses 'A' are mandatory in CIF; (C) is the minimum, (A) is for CIP.

entries.title: CFR (cost and freight)
entries.in_plain_words: Like CIF but the buyer arranges its own insurance.
entries.in_detail: Seller pays freight to the destination port; risk passes at loading; buyer insures. Common alternative when the buyer wants its own insurer.

entries.title: FCA (free carrier) - for ISO tanks, trucks and containers
entries.in_plain_words: The seller hands the goods to the buyer's carrier at a named place.
entries.in_detail: Used for containerised or road/rail loads such as ISO tanks and flexitanks. Delivery occurs when goods are handed to the carrier at the named place; the seller clears export.

entries.title: Joint-working / tandem agreement
entries.in_plain_words: Two intermediaries agree to work a deal together.
entries.in_detail: Defines roles, who holds which contact, how the commission is shared and what happens if one party leaves. Often an alternative to long broker chains.

entries.title: Voyage charter party
entries.in_plain_words: A contract to hire a ship for one trip.
entries.in_detail: Between shipowner and charterer: vessel, cargo, ports, freight, laytime, demurrage, deadfreight. Charter-party terms flow through to the sale contract via laytime and demurrage clauses. For liquid cargoes tanker-specific standard forms exist.

entries.title: Time charter and contract of affreightment (COA)
entries.in_plain_words: Hiring a ship for a period, or agreeing to ship many cargoes over time.
entries.in_detail: Time charter: the charterer controls the ship for a period and pays hire. COA: the owner agrees to carry a volume over time on agreed terms. Note: COA also abbreviates 'certificate of analysis'.

entries.title: Storage and terminal agreement
entries.in_plain_words: A contract to store and handle oil at a port terminal.
entries.in_detail: Covers tank allocation, throughput, handling fees, heating, quality, losses and access. Terminal receipts are evidence of custody.

entries.title: Offtake, long-term supply and tolling agreements
entries.in_plain_words: Long contracts that secure supply or processing capacity.
entries.in_detail: Offtake: buyer commits to take product over years. Supply agreement: producer commits volume. Tolling: a processor treats the customer's feedstock for a fee, the customer keeps title.

entries.title: Addenda and amendments
entries.in_plain_words: Written changes to a signed contract.
entries.in_detail: Changes should be in writing, signed and refer to the original. Keep the LC consistent with amendments.

entries.title: Clause: parties, product and specification
entries.in_plain_words: Who is buying and selling what, and to what quality.
entries.in_detail: Exact legal entities and addresses; description of the product including feedstock type and origin; specification parameters with limits and test methods; what counts as off-spec.

entries.title: Clause: quantity and tolerance
entries.in_plain_words: How much, and how much more or less is acceptable.
entries.in_detail: Nominal quantity; tolerance (e.g. plus or minus a percentage) and who has the option; how quantity is measured (shore tank, vessel figures) and which figure governs; loss allowances; partial shipments. Keep consistent with LC tolerance (UCP 600 art. 30).

entries.title: Clause: price and pricing formula
entries.in_plain_words: How the price is calculated.
entries.in_detail: Fixed price or floating price based on a benchmark plus premium or discount; pricing period (quotational period); currency; provisional invoice and final adjustment; treatment of benchmark changes. Not simply 'tons times average benchmark': the contract defines which benchmark, which days and which quantity.
entries.verify_note: Original reduced the invoice to 'tons x Argus average'.

entries.title: Clause: delivery, title and risk transfer
entries.in_plain_words: When the goods become the buyer's responsibility and property.
entries.in_detail: Incoterm and place of delivery; moment risk passes; moment title passes (at loading, on payment or on documents); retention of title until paid.

entries.title: Clause: laycan and nominations
entries.in_plain_words: The loading window and how the ship is announced.
entries.in_detail: Laycan = laydays (earliest date the ship may be ready to load) and cancelling date (latest). Notice periods for estimated arrival, nomination of the vessel by the party responsible, acceptance or rejection and substitution. Missing the window can allow the other side to cancel or claim.
entries.verify_note: Original defined laycan only as 'exact days of loading'.

entries.title: Clause: vessel requirements
entries.in_plain_words: What kind of ship is acceptable.
entries.in_detail: Age, class, flag, ownership and sanctions screening, P&I cover, ISM and ISPS compliance, tank condition and coating, pumping and heating capability, vetting, draft limits at ports. Verify the vessel's IMO number and history independently.

entries.title: Clause: laytime, demurrage, despatch and deadfreight
entries.in_plain_words: Time allowed in port and who pays for delays or unused space.
entries.in_detail: Laytime: time allowed to load or discharge. Demurrage: compensation when laytime is exceeded. Despatch: reward for finishing early. Deadfreight: freight owed for cargo space booked but not used, e.g. shortfall. Rates, notice of readiness and time bars are set in the charter party and flow through the sale contract.
entries.verify_note: Original described demurrage and deadfreight as fines for delay.

entries.title: Clause: inspection and sampling
entries.in_plain_words: Who measures and tests the cargo, and whose result counts.
entries.in_detail: Names the independent inspector (not a single brand by default), sampling method, sealed samples, whether load-port results are final and binding, carve-outs for fraud or manifest error, procedure for disputes, retained-sample period and cost allocation.
entries.verify_note: Original wrote 'SGS final and binding'; the inspector is whoever the contract names.

entries.title: Clause: quality deviations, penalties, rejection and claims
entries.in_plain_words: What happens if the oil is not as agreed.
entries.in_detail: Penalty or price-adjustment scale for deviations, limits beyond which the buyer can reject, replacement rights, claim notice periods, umpire laboratory. Example numbers in contracts are deal-specific.

entries.title: Clause: sustainability compliance
entries.in_plain_words: Promises that the product counts under the rules it is sold for.
entries.in_detail: Seller maintains valid ISCC (or other recognised scheme) certification; delivers a proof of sustainability with each cargo; honours mass balance and declared GHG values; no mixing with virgin or non-compliant material; records in the Union Database as required; audit and information rights; indemnity and termination if certification is suspended; documents delivered as a payment condition.

entries.title: Clause: change in law and regulatory events
entries.in_plain_words: What happens if the rules change during the contract.
entries.in_detail: Allows renegotiation, suspension or termination if a law, export ban or scheme rule changes (for example export bans in producing countries, caps on feedstock eligibility, changes in national transposition of RED III).

entries.title: Clause: payment and LC terms
entries.in_plain_words: How and when the buyer pays and when the LC must be open.
entries.in_detail: LC opening deadline relative to the loading window; type (at sight, deferred, confirmed, transferable); issuing bank standards; amount including tolerance; document list matching the sale contract; expiry and place of presentation; who bears banking charges; consequences of late opening (seller may refuse to load and claim).

entries.title: Clause: documents
entries.in_plain_words: Which papers the seller must deliver and when.
entries.in_detail: List of documents (B/L, invoice, certificates, sustainability documents, insurance for CIF), number of originals and copies, timelines, handling when originals arrive after the ship (letter of indemnity form), consistency requirements.

entries.title: Clause: insurance
entries.in_plain_words: Who insures the cargo and for how much.
entries.in_detail: Responsible party, level of cover, insured value, loss payee. In CIF the seller procures at least the Incoterms minimum.

entries.title: Clause: force majeure
entries.in_plain_words: Relief for events outside the parties' control.
entries.in_detail: Defines events (e.g. war, strikes, port closure, government export bans), notice, mitigation, duration and termination right. Decide upfront whether regulatory export bans count.

entries.title: Clause: sanctions, anti-bribery and AML
entries.in_plain_words: Promises that the deal is clean and a right to stop if it is not.
entries.in_detail: Warranties that no party or vessel is sanctioned; no bribery; compliance with AML law; right to suspend or terminate without liability; information duties.

entries.title: Clause: default and termination
entries.in_plain_words: What counts as a breach and what the other side can do.
entries.in_detail: Events of default, cure periods, termination, liquidated damages, set-off.

entries.title: Clause: liability and indemnities
entries.in_plain_words: Who pays for what and what is capped.
entries.in_detail: Limits on consequential loss, caps, specific indemnities (for example for invalid sustainability documents or sanctions).

entries.title: Clause: governing law and dispute resolution
entries.in_plain_words: Which country's law applies and where disputes are decided.
entries.in_detail: English law is very common in commodity trading, but not mandatory. Options: law of England with London arbitration (LCIA or FOSFA rules); Singapore law with SIAC; Malaysian law with AIAC in Kuala Lumpur; Spanish law with a Spanish or ICC arbitration; any other agreed law. Arbitral awards are widely enforceable under the New York Convention.
entries.verify_note: Original said English law 'must always' be stipulated.

entries.title: Clauses: confidentiality, assignment, notices, entire agreement, amendments, counterparts
entries.in_plain_words: The standard legal housekeeping clauses.
entries.in_detail: Confidentiality; whether a party may assign the contract; how notices are validly sent; entire agreement; written amendment; severability; electronic signatures and counterparts; language.

entries.title: Clause: brokerage
entries.in_plain_words: Whether and how the broker's fee appears in the sale contract.
entries.in_detail: The seller or buyer may state that a broker was involved and who pays, or leave the broker out and use a separate agreement. Naming the broker's fee in a contract seen by both sides may conflict with confidentiality. It does not by itself instruct a bank to pay.
entries.verify_note: Original said the IMFPA stapled to the SPA lets the bank process the fee automatically.

entries.title: Bill of lading (B/L)
entries.in_plain_words: The carrier's receipt for the cargo, the transport contract and the key to collect the goods.
entries.in_detail: Three functions: receipt for goods, evidence of the contract of carriage, and document of title (whoever holds a properly endorsed original can claim delivery). Normally issued as a set of originals. Under UCP 600 art. 20 and 27 the credit usually asks for a 'clean shipped on board' B/L: 'shipped on board' and 'clean' are two separate attributes. Remarks about apparent condition make it 'claused'.
options_and_variants: Straight B/L: Consignee named
Order B/L: Negotiable by endorsement
Bearer B/L: Holder is entitled
Clean / claused (foul): No adverse remarks / with remarks
Shipped on board / received for shipment: Loaded versus merely received
Charter-party B/L: Issued under a charter, UCP art. 22
Sea waybill: Non-negotiable
Electronic B/L: Digital equivalent
risks_and_red_flags: Forged or altered originals
Remarks that make it unacceptable to the bank
entries.verify_note: Original wrote 'CLEAN ON BOARD' as a single stamp.

entries.title: Switch bill of lading
entries.in_plain_words: A trader replaces the original B/L with a new one in its own name.
entries.in_detail: Used to hide the identity of the original supplier or loading details from the buyer, or to change ports. Legitimate in some trades, but it can obscure origin and traceability, which clashes with chain-of-custody rules for certified sustainable material, and it is a known tool in fraud.
risks_and_red_flags: Used to disguise origin
Conflict with traceability duties

entries.title: Electronic bill of lading (eBL)
entries.in_plain_words: A B/L issued and transferred digitally on a platform.
entries.in_detail: Adoption is growing from a low base. Whether a bank accepts it depends on what the LC says and on the rules it is subject to (eUCP); many LC-based deals still use paper originals. Legal recognition varies by country.
entries.verify_note: Check platform, applicable law and the LC text for each deal.

entries.title: Sea waybill
entries.in_plain_words: A non-negotiable shipping receipt.
entries.in_detail: Cargo is delivered to the named consignee without presenting an original. Faster than a B/L but not a document of title and less useful as security.

entries.title: Delivery order (D/O)
entries.in_plain_words: An instruction to release cargo to a named receiver.
entries.in_detail: Issued by the holder of the B/L, or the carrier's agent, to the terminal or vessel to deliver cargo to a party. Used when cargo is sold on while in transit.

entries.title: Letter of indemnity (LOI, indemnity)
entries.in_plain_words: The buyer promises the shipowner to cover losses if cargo is released without the original B/L.
entries.in_detail: Used when the ship arrives before the documents. Normally countersigned by a bank and in a form the shipowner or its P&I club accepts. The sale contract should say when and in what form it is given. Improvised or unsupported indemnities are a known weak point. Not the same as 'letter of intent'.
risks_and_red_flags: Cargo released to the wrong party
Unbacked indemnity

entries.title: Notice of readiness (NOR)
entries.in_plain_words: The ship tells the port it is ready to load or discharge.
entries.in_detail: Starts the laytime clock under the charter party, subject to its terms. Validity conditions are contract-specific.

entries.title: Statement of facts and laytime calculation
entries.in_plain_words: The time log of the port call and the calculation of time used.
entries.in_detail: Records arrival, NOR, berthing, start and end of loading, delays. The laytime calculation derives demurrage or despatch from it.

entries.title: Mate's receipt and cargo manifest
entries.in_plain_words: The ship's record of what was loaded.
entries.in_detail: The mate's receipt precedes the B/L. The manifest lists the cargo for customs and port authorities.

entries.title: Tank inspection / cleanliness certificate
entries.in_plain_words: A check that the ship's tanks are fit for the cargo.
entries.in_detail: Done by an independent inspector before loading. Residues, contaminated coatings or water can ruin a cargo. Also record remaining on board (ROB) and on board quantity (OBQ).

entries.title: Shore-tank and ship figures
entries.in_plain_words: The measurements that decide how much was loaded.
entries.in_detail: Inspector measures shore tanks before and after loading and the ship's tanks (ullage, temperature, density). Differences between shore and ship figures are normal within a margin; large differences need explanation.

entries.title: Vessel documents and vetting
entries.in_plain_words: Papers and checks that prove the ship is real and acceptable.
entries.in_detail: IMO number, flag and ownership, class certificate, P&I cover, ISM and ISPS certificates, tank suitability, inspection history. Cross-check the IMO number and AIS track in public ship databases and screen against sanctions lists.
risks_and_red_flags: Ship scrapped, renamed or elsewhere
Sanctioned owner or manager

entries.title: Cargo insurance and Institute Cargo Clauses
entries.in_plain_words: Insurance for loss or damage to the goods in transit.
entries.in_detail: Institute Cargo Clauses (A) cover all risks, (B) named perils, (C) a narrower set. Under CIF the seller must provide at least (C) at 110% of price; CIP requires (A). War and strikes clauses are separate. The certificate or policy is a banking document under UCP art. 28.

entries.title: Commercial invoice (provisional and final)
entries.in_plain_words: The seller's bill for the cargo.
entries.in_detail: Under an LC the goods description must match the credit exactly (UCP art. 18). Typically a provisional invoice at shipment and a final invoice after price or quantity adjustments; credit and debit notes correct differences.

entries.title: Packing list
entries.in_plain_words: A list of how the goods are packed.
entries.in_detail: Relevant for ISO tanks, drums or IBCs; gives container or tank numbers, weights and seals.

entries.title: Certificates of quality and quantity
entries.in_plain_words: Independent inspector's results on quality and on weight.
entries.in_detail: Two separate certificates, plus shore-tank and ship-figure reports. Issued by an independent inspection company, not by a government. Bind the parties only to the extent the contract says so.
entries.verify_note: Original called it an 'official verdict'.

entries.title: Certificate of analysis (COA)
entries.in_plain_words: A laboratory's analysis of a sample.
entries.in_detail: Shows tested parameters and results, ideally linked to a specific lot, tank and sampling record. Value depends on the lab's independence. Not the same as 'contract of affreightment', also abbreviated COA.

entries.title: Sampling, sealed and retained samples, umpire analysis
entries.in_plain_words: Taking, sealing and keeping samples so quality disputes can be settled.
entries.in_detail: Several sets are sealed and signed: seller's, buyer's, inspector's and sometimes a referee set. They are retained for an agreed period. If results differ, a referee or umpire laboratory may decide, depending on the contract.

entries.title: Key quality parameters
entries.in_plain_words: The measurements that decide whether the oil is acceptable.
entries.in_detail: Typical parameters (limits are buyer-specific): free fatty acids (FFA), moisture, insoluble impurities, unsaponifiable matter, total contamination, density, iodine and saponification values, sulphur, phosphorus, metals (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium), chlorine and other halogens, polymerised matter, colour. Plants making hydrotreated fuels tend to be stricter on phosphorus, metals and chlorine.

entries.title: Independent inspectors and laboratories
entries.in_plain_words: Companies that sample, measure and certify cargoes.
entries.in_detail: Examples include SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas (including Inspectorate), Saybolt, AmSpec, Cotecna and Control Union. Names are appointed by the contract. Some are also ISCC certification bodies, which is a different job from cargo inspection.

entries.title: Certificate of origin
entries.in_plain_words: A paper stating where the goods come from.
entries.in_detail: Issued by an authorised chamber or authority. Preferential origin can reduce import duty under trade agreements; non-preferential is for statistics and rules. It is not a sustainability origin proof.

entries.title: Export declaration
entries.in_plain_words: The customs paper that clears the goods to leave the country.
entries.in_detail: In Malaysia the export declaration is filed with Royal Malaysian Customs (customs form K2). The exporter or its agent files it. Confirm current forms and procedures with customs or a licensed agent.
entries.verify_note: Verify form names and requirements with Malaysian customs.

entries.title: Import declaration
entries.in_plain_words: The customs paper that clears goods into the importing country.
entries.in_detail: In the EU a customs declaration under the Union Customs Code, with an EORI number, tariff classification, origin and customs value. Import duty, VAT and any trade-defence duties depend on classification and origin.

entries.title: Tariff classification (HS / CN codes)
entries.in_plain_words: The code that says what the product is for customs.
entries.in_detail: A customs decision that differs by country. Indonesia's POME oil, HAPOR and EFB oil were cited under HS 2306.60.90 in market reports. UCO is often classified in Chapter 15, but verify. In the EU, binding tariff information can confirm classification. Wrong codes can change duties, permits and whether a product counts as a waste or a commodity.
entries.verify_note: Verify codes with customs authorities in both countries.

entries.title: Malaysia: export-side documents and licences
entries.in_plain_words: What a Malaysian exporter needs besides the cargo papers.
entries.in_detail: A customs declaration (form K2) filed with Royal Malaysian Customs; for crude palm oil, processed palm oil and sludge palm oil a customs export licence under the Customs (Prohibition on Exports) Order 2017; MPOB licences for sludge palm oil and used palm cooking oil dealers (selling and moving, buying and moving, storing, exporting) with monthly volume declarations. Malaysia had no export duty on UCO or POME oil as of an October 2025 report, but duties were under consideration. MPOB was reviewing standards to separate UCO from SPO and planned an official UCO reference price in early 2026.
entries.verify_note: Verified on 18 Oct 2026 for licensing and the export licence; confirm form names and duties with Customs and MPOB.

entries.title: Transport modes and equipment
entries.in_plain_words: How the oil physically moves.
entries.in_detail: Palm-based oils solidify at ambient temperature, so heating is a recurring requirement.
options_and_variants: Chemical or vegetable-oil parcel tanker: Deep-sea cargoes, sizes from small coastal to large
ISO tank: Containerised liquid tank, FCA-type terms
Flexitank: Single-use bladder in a container; heating limits
Drums and IBCs: Small lots
Road tanker: Collection and port transfers
Rail tank car: Inland movement
Barge: River and coastal
Pipeline: Normally only within terminals or port-to-plant links

entries.title: RED II - Directive (EU) 2018/2001
entries.in_plain_words: The EU law that sets renewable-energy rules, including which feedstocks count for transport fuels.
entries.in_detail: Sets sustainability and GHG criteria for biofuels, the Annex IX list of feedstocks (Part A advanced, Part B limited), the cap on Part B, and the option of counting some feedstocks twice towards targets. Amended by RED III.

entries.title: RED III - Directive (EU) 2023/2413
entries.in_plain_words: The 2023 update that raises EU renewable targets and must be written into national law.
entries.in_detail: A directive: each Member State transposes it, so rules differ by country (obligation type, multipliers, caps, classifications). Transport options include a renewable-energy share or a GHG-intensity reduction (Spain's draft aims for 17.6% GHG reduction by 2030 against 14.5% in the directive). Check each destination country's current law.
entries.verify_note: Transposition status moves quickly; check the destination country's law.

entries.title: Annex IX Part A and Part B
entries.in_plain_words: The EU list of waste and residue feedstocks that get special treatment.
entries.in_detail: Part A: advanced feedstocks, e.g. palm oil mill effluent (POME) oil and empty palm fruit bunches, which count towards an advanced sub-target. Part B: only used cooking oil and category 1 and 2 animal fats. PFAD is not in Annex IX. The list can be amended by delegated act.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it. Annex IX scope can change by delegated act.

entries.title: Annex IX Part B cap (1.7%)
entries.in_plain_words: A ceiling on how much UCO and animal fat each country can count.
entries.in_detail: The cap is 1.7% of the energy content of transport fuels per Member State, which limits eligible volume regardless of supply. Member States may seek to adjust it with justification and the Commission can review it. Industry bodies were asking in March 2026 for a review and consideration of removing it in the next revision.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Double counting - country by country
entries.in_plain_words: Some countries let certain feedstocks count twice towards targets; many are moving away from it.
entries.in_detail: Not a uniform EU rule in 2026. The Netherlands proposed abolishing it for Annex IX feedstocks; Germany is phasing it out for some Part A fuels; Mediterranean countries kept it in 2026. Where it ends, UCO value rests more on its GHG savings. Always ask which Member State the fuel will be used in.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/996
entries.in_plain_words: The EU rules on how sustainability and GHG claims are verified.
entries.in_detail: Sets rules for verification, audits and the role of voluntary schemes and certification bodies. Useful reference when a contract says 'compliant with RED'.
entries.verify_note: Confirm the regulation number and current consolidated text.

entries.title: Voluntary schemes recognised by the EU
entries.in_plain_words: Private certification schemes the Commission accepts as proof of RED compliance.
entries.in_detail: Names commonly cited: ISCC EU, REDcert-EU, 2BSvs, Better Biomass, Bonsucro EU, RSB EU RED, RTRS EU RED, SURE-EU, KZR INiG. Recognition is time-limited and can lapse. RSPO is a palm-sustainability scheme, not a general EU-recognised proof for UCO.
entries.verify_note: Check the Commission's current list of recognised schemes.

entries.title: ISCC EU
entries.in_plain_words: The most common certification scheme for UCO and POME sold into the EU.
entries.in_detail: Companies in the chain are audited by independent certification bodies; certificates are valid for one year and re-audited annually. Audits look at traceability, mass balance and GHG data. Verify counterparties in the ISCC public database.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: ISCC PLUS
entries.in_plain_words: ISCC's scheme for markets outside EU fuel rules, such as materials and bio-circular products.
entries.in_detail: Used for non-RED applications. Not a substitute for ISCC EU when material must count under EU fuel rules. Check which scope a certificate covers.

entries.title: ISCC roles in the supply chain
entries.in_plain_words: Each company in the chain has a defined role and must be certified for it.
entries.in_detail: Points of origin (restaurants, food plants) are not individually certified and sign a self-declaration to the collecting point. The collecting point is the first certified operator for UCO. Other roles: first gathering point (agricultural biomass, not UCO), trader, trader with storage, processing unit (pretreatment or refinery), biofuel producer. Collecting points and conversion plants are recognised weak spots for fraud. Brokers who never take title or custody are generally outside the chain of custody; confirm in ISCC documents.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Point-of-origin self-declaration
entries.in_plain_words: A restaurant or plant signs a statement that the oil is its own used oil.
entries.in_detail: Declares that the material supplied was generated by the point of origin. ISCC can publish exclusions of points of origin found to make false declarations. Self-declaration is only as good as the collector's checks.
risks_and_red_flags: Same volume declared twice
Virgin oil sold as used oil
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Mass balance
entries.in_plain_words: An accounting method that lets sustainable and other material mix as long as volumes balance on paper.
entries.in_detail: Allowed under strict conditions in defined periods and sites. Its weakness is that physical product is not tracked, so records and audits carry the weight; fraud can exploit multiple claims. Operators must keep consistent inputs, outputs and certificates.
risks_and_red_flags: Multiple claiming of the same material

entries.title: Proof of sustainability (PoS)
entries.in_plain_words: The document that travels with a cargo and says it is sustainable.
entries.in_detail: Issued by a certified supplier for a specific consignment, naming supplier, recipient, material, quantity, certificate numbers and GHG data. It is transaction-specific: a 'sample' or old PoS only shows the format. Ask for the supplier's certificate number and verify it independently.
entries.verify_note: Original asked for a 'draft of past PoS' as proof of capability; that does not verify anything.

entries.title: Union Database for Biofuels (UDB)
entries.in_plain_words: The EU register where biofuel transactions are recorded for traceability.
entries.in_detail: Economic operators record transactions in the Union Database so authorities can trace consignments. Roles and obligations depend on position in the chain; confirm who records what with the destination plant and the certification scheme.
entries.verify_note: Confirm current UDB obligations and user roles.

entries.title: GHG savings and calculation
entries.in_plain_words: The percentage of emissions saved compared with fossil fuel.
entries.in_detail: Calculated with default or actual values; minimum savings thresholds depend on when the installation started operating (e.g. 65% for installations from 2021 under RED II). The value appears in the PoS. Wrong GHG data is a source of disputes.

entries.title: ReFuelEU Aviation - Regulation (EU) 2023/2405
entries.in_plain_words: The EU mandate for sustainable aviation fuel.
entries.in_detail: Sets rising SAF blending requirements. Eligibility rules exclude PFAD and other palm- and soy-derived feedstocks according to analyses of the rules. This increases competition for UCO and Annex IX feedstocks.

entries.title: FuelEU Maritime - Regulation (EU) 2023/1805
entries.in_plain_words: The EU limit on the greenhouse-gas intensity of fuel used by ships.
entries.in_detail: Phased limits on GHG intensity; a penalty of 2,400 euros per tonne of VLSFO equivalent was reported for exceeding it. Adds demand for sustainable bunker fuels.
entries.verify_note: Check penalty and timeline in the regulation.

entries.title: EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)
entries.in_plain_words: A rule that keeps deforestation-linked commodities out of the EU.
entries.in_detail: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115, amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2650. Application: 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators and traders, and 30 June 2027 for micro and small operators (micro and small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation follow the earlier date). The Commission's simplification review of May 2026 kept the dates and said no further delay or reopening of the text is planned; commentary published in the last days still treats 30 December 2026 as the deadline. A delegated act adjusting the product list (Annex I) is under way, adding some palm derivatives and exemptions that include waste; products newly added to Annex I are reported to come into scope on 30 December 2027, which may be the source of 'end of 2027' dates you may hear. Palm oil is in scope with its derivatives. Whether a given UCO or POME oil is in scope or exempt waste or residue depends on classification and the final delegated act.
entries.verify_note: Checked on 18 Oct 2026 against legal summaries and trade press. If a buyer cites a different date, ask for the source.

entries.title: Spain: biofuel framework
entries.in_plain_words: Spain's national rules that decide what is bought and counted.
entries.in_detail: Royal Decree 1085/2015 on biofuels; Royal Decree 5/2026 sets the 2026 minimum target at 12% biofuels by energy content. A draft decree transposing RED III (public consultation in early 2026) would aim for a 17.6% GHG reduction by 2030 and replace RD 1085/2015 from 1 January 2027. APPA asked the ministry to request a higher Part B cap. The Spanish biofuel certification system is run by the market regulator.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it. Final approval of the new decree was not confirmed; check the BOE.

entries.title: Other national transpositions of RED III
entries.in_plain_words: What other big markets are doing.
entries.in_detail: Germany: draft allowed crediting some POME-based biofuels placed on the market before 2027 and is phasing out double counting for some Part A fuels. Netherlands: proposal to abolish double counting. Italy: transposed with effect from February 2026. Always check the law of the country where the fuel will be consumed.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: UK and US schemes
entries.in_plain_words: Other big demand markets for UCO.
entries.in_detail: UK: Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation with its own rules on waste feedstocks. US: Renewable Fuel Standard credits (RINs), California Low Carbon Fuel Standard and federal clean-fuel production credits whose feedstock-origin rules have changed recently. Rules differ from the EU.
entries.verify_note: Not verified in this version; research before targeting these markets.

entries.title: RSPO
entries.in_plain_words: The sustainability certification body for palm oil.
entries.in_detail: Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil certifies palm oil and palm products and offers supply-chain models such as identity preserved, segregated and mass balance. It is relevant for palm products and mills producing POME oil; it does not certify UCO.
entries.verify_note: Confirm RSPO's relation to EU recognition for residues.

entries.title: MSPO and ISPO
entries.in_plain_words: National sustainable-palm standards of Malaysia and Indonesia.
entries.in_detail: MSPO (Malaysia) covers most plantations; a Malaysian official said about 87% of plantations were certified. ISPO is Indonesia's equivalent. They are national standards, not EU fuel-compliance proof.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Indonesia: crude POME and UCO export ban
entries.in_plain_words: Indonesia does not let crude POME and crude UCO leave the country.
entries.in_detail: First restricted in January 2025 and confirmed as maintained in February 2026. Refined grades continued to be exported. Drafts earlier required export permits and domestic market obligations for POME oil, HAPOR and EFB oil. The aim is to secure feedstock for biodiesel and aviation fuel.
risks_and_red_flags: Cargoes described as Indonesian crude POME or UCO
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Malaysia: MPOB oversight of UCO and sludge palm oil (SPO)
entries.in_plain_words: Malaysia licenses and monitors the collection, storage and export of used palm oil and sludge.
entries.in_detail: Under the MPOB (Licensing) Regulations 2005, used palm cooking oil is classified as sludge palm oil, and four activities are licensed: selling and moving, buying and moving, storing, and exporting. Exporting crude palm oil, processed palm oil and sludge palm oil also needs a customs export licence under the Customs (Prohibition on Exports) Order 2017. Collectors declare monthly volumes to MPOB. Since 2025 MPOB has been reviewing its standards to separate UCO from SPO and has announced a crackdown on export fraud, so classification is in flux. Practical rule: declare exactly what the product is under the rules in force, never relabel a product to fit a licence, and ask the exporter for its MPOB licence numbers and customs export licence. Misdeclaring goods in a customs declaration is an offence that can bring penalties and seizure (Indonesian customs, for example, seized a UCO shipment declared under the wrong tariff code in 2022); confirm the exact Malaysian consequences with a customs lawyer. Diverting subsidised cooking oil into UCO exports is prohibited.
risks_and_red_flags: Asking an exporter to relabel UCO as SPO, or the reverse, to fit a licence
Missing MPOB licence or customs export licence
entries.verify_note: Verified on 18 Oct 2026: classification under the 2005 regulations and the customs export licence requirement. Not verified: specific seizure rules on the K2 declaration or different duties for SPO and UCO.

entries.title: Malaysia: export duty on UCO and POME oil
entries.in_plain_words: Whether Malaysia taxes exports of these oils.
entries.in_detail: As of an October 2025 report there was no export duty on UCO or POME oil, while crude palm oil carries an export duty. MPOB said duties on waste oils were being considered. Check the finance ministry for the current position.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Is UCO a waste, a by-product or a commodity?
entries.in_plain_words: The legal label changes which rules apply.
entries.in_detail: Different countries classify used cooking oil differently (Malaysian licensing rules treat used palm cooking oil as sludge palm oil, and MPOB is reviewing how to separate UCO from SPO). Waste classification can trigger waste-shipment, permit and EUDR-exemption questions. Ask for the classification used in both export and import documents.

entries.title: Enforcement and fraud pressure on UCO
entries.in_plain_words: Authorities are actively checking this market.
entries.in_detail: In March 2026 the European Commission confirmed a probe into possible fraud in advanced biodiesel; ISCC withdrew certificates for mislabelling and sanctioned a certification body for documents on a plant that did not exist; a Dutch plant owner was fined 5 million euros; Indonesia and Malaysia are tightening controls. Expect strong buyer due diligence.
entries.verify_note: Verified by web search on 17 Oct 2026; re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Sanctions
entries.in_plain_words: Legal bans on dealing with certain people, companies, ships and countries.
entries.in_detail: EU, UN, US and UK regimes differ. Screen counterparties, owners (UBO), banks, ships, ports and cargo origin against each list that may apply. EU sanctions bind EU nationals even when they act outside the EU. Evasion patterns involve intermediaries, relabelled origin and ship-to-ship transfers. Penalties can be personal.
entries.verify_note: Confirm exposure with a qualified lawyer.

entries.title: AML and KYC
entries.in_plain_words: Rules to stop dirty money moving through trade.
entries.in_detail: FATF standards implemented through national law (e.g. EU AML directives and Spain's Law 10/2010, Malaysia's AMLA). Banks and some intermediaries have duties to identify customers, owners and the source of funds. Trade-based money laundering uses over- and under-invoicing and phantom shipments.

entries.title: Anti-bribery
