entries.in_plain_words: Rules against paying officials or business partners for advantages.
entries.in_detail: Malaysia's MACC Act section 17A creates corporate liability for corruption by associated persons unless adequate procedures exist; the UK Bribery Act and US FCPA also reach conduct abroad. Commission payments to agents are a known risk area; large traders have cut or tightened middlemen after corruption probes.

entries.title: Data protection
entries.in_plain_words: Rules on handling personal data such as passports.
entries.in_detail: GDPR (EU) and PDPA (Malaysia) apply to KYC packs. Share the minimum, store securely, and set retention limits.

entries.title: Commercial-agent law
entries.in_plain_words: Some countries give agents special rights, such as compensation on termination.
entries.in_detail: EU Directive 86/653/EEC and its national laws (Spain's Ley 12/1992) protect self-employed commercial agents. Whether a broker falls within them depends on facts and the contract's law. Take advice before choosing the structure.

entries.title: Arbitration institutions and venues
entries.in_plain_words: Where disputes are decided.
entries.in_detail: Common choices include LCIA and FOSFA (London), SIAC (Singapore), AIAC (Kuala Lumpur), ICC and HKIAC. The New York Convention helps enforce awards across most trading countries. Pick a neutral seat and institution that both sides can use.

entries.title: Entity, tax and licensing for a broker
entries.in_plain_words: Which company earns the fee, what tax applies and what permits you need.
entries.in_detail: Choice of entity and country (e.g. Malaysian company or Spanish company), VAT on services, withholding on cross-border commissions, permanent-establishment risk, visa and work-permit status, and whether brokering needs any licence. Not covered in this version.
entries.verify_note: Needs an accountant and a lawyer familiar with Malaysia and Spain.

entries.title: Who is who in a deal: principal, mandate holder, broker, introducer, employee
entries.in_plain_words: Five roles that tell you what each person in a deal really is.
entries.in_detail: Label every actor with one of these roles before trusting anything they say. The principal is the party that signs the sales contract, issues the invoice and is the beneficiary or applicant of the letter of credit. Everyone else is an intermediary of some kind.
options_and_variants: Principal: Owns the goods and the title (seller) or pays for them (buyer)
Mandate holder: Has written authority from a principal to offer or seek goods in its name
Broker: Connects parties for a commission, with no title and no mandate; this is your position
Introducer: Knows someone; no title, no mandate and no documented fee, so there is no authority to verify
Employee: Acts within the powers of a principal's role; always check signing authority

entries.title: Physical and certified supply-chain roles
entries.in_plain_words: Who actually handles the oil.
entries.in_detail: Point of origin, collector (collecting point), aggregator or trader with storage, processing unit (pretreatment or refinery), biofuel producer, supplier or blender, obligated party. Each needs the right certification for its role.

entries.title: Service providers
entries.in_plain_words: Companies that support a deal without owning it.
entries.in_detail: Independent inspectors and labs; certification bodies; shipbrokers and ship agents; terminal operators; banks (issuing, advising, confirming, nominated, negotiating, reimbursing); lawyers and arbitrators; insurers and P&I clubs. Keep each role's job separate.

entries.title: Catalogue of intermediary chains
entries.in_plain_words: The usual shapes a deal chain can take, from safest to most dangerous.
entries.in_detail: A deal chain runs from the original seller to the final buyer. On the seller side the safest shape is a producer or collector selling directly to the plant. Next comes a chain of title, where a collector sells to a trader who sells to the plant: each party buys and resells, so the certificates must be continuous. A broker standing between two principals is your target position and is low to moderate risk when you hold a written commission agreement. A mandate holder presenting the seller's offer is moderate risk and needs the mandate verified. A mandate holder who passes the mandate on to another mandate holder is high risk, because the first mandate must allow it. Several brokers in series, with no mandate, are high risk: commissions stack and nobody has authority. Introducers who only know someone are very high risk. On the buyer side the safest shape is the plant's own purchasing employee, then a group trading company buying for the group's plants, then a buying agent with a written mandate. A trader buying to resell is a real principal but depends on finding its own buyer, so its payment capacity needs proof. Chains of brokers or mandates on the buyer side are high risk, and a buyer with no plant, no offtake and no bank behind it is a red flag. Three special patterns cut across both sides: a string of principals selling the same cargo down the line, a circular trade, and a phantom principal.
options_and_variants: Direct sale: Producer or collector sells to the plant: lowest risk
Chain of title: Collector sells to trader, trader sells to plant: moderate, certificates must be continuous
Broker between two principals: Your target position: low to moderate with a written commission agreement
Mandate holder presents the offer: Moderate: verify the mandate with the issuer
Mandate passed to another mandate holder: High: the first mandate must allow it
Brokers in series: High: commissions stack and nobody has authority
Introducer chain: Very high: no authority to verify
Plant purchasing employee: Lowest risk on the buyer side: confirm signing authority
Group trading company buying for plants: Low to moderate: check who pays and who receives
Buying agent with a mandate: Moderate: verify the mandate
Trader buying to resell: Moderate to high: ask for proof of a final buyer and of payment capacity
Chain of brokers on the buyer side: High: the real buyer is hidden
Buyer with no plant or offtake: Red flag: cannot show funds or a bank
String of principals on one cargo: The same cargo sold down the line, each holding title for a moment: moderate to high
Circular trade: The flow returns to the starting party, with no real end buyer: red flag
Phantom principal: A party posing as seller that has nothing: high risk
Dual agency: One intermediary acting for both sides without saying so: high risk

entries.title: End-to-end deal lifecycle
entries.in_plain_words: The steps of a deal from first contact to cash.
entries.in_detail: Order varies: corporate buyers often go NDA, onboarding, spec and sample, term sheet, SPA, LC; broker chains go SCO, ICPO, NCNDA/IMFPA, PoP and PoF, SPA, LC.
options_and_variants: 0 KYC: Identify and screen parties
1 Demand: RFQ with full data
2 Offer: SCO or FCO
3 Negotiation: Price, quantity, quality, inspector, Incoterm, window, payment, law
4 Contract: SPA or call-off
5 Payment security: LC opened and checked
6 Logistics: Nominations, inspector appointed
7 Loading: Inspection, B/L
8 Transit: Documents via banks
9 Discharge: Inspection, claims
10 Payment and commission: Documents presented, bank pays, fee paid

entries.title: The four flows model
entries.in_plain_words: Every deal is four things happening at once.
entries.in_detail: Physical flow (the oil), document flow (contract, B/L, certificates), money flow (LC, payment, commission), sustainability flow (certificates, PoS, mass balance). Fraud appears when the flows tell different stories: paper without cargo, cargo not as certified, payment without valid documents. Ask: can I prove all four tell the same story?

entries.title: How to map a chain
entries.in_plain_words: A short method to find out who is really in a deal.
entries.in_detail: 1) Ask who signs the SPA, who invoices and who is LC beneficiary. 2) Get the document proving each link (title or mandate). 3) Verify the physical operator's ISCC certificate in the public database. 4) Check that volume matches capacity. 5) Check no party appears twice and that related entities are identified. 6) Rule of thumb: more than two undocumented layers between you and a principal on either side is a stop.

entries.title: Mandate verification checklist
entries.in_plain_words: What to check before relying on someone's mandate.
entries.in_detail: Issuer exists (registry extract); signer has power; mandate names product, volume, price mechanism, validity, commission, exclusivity and sub-mandate permission; confirm with issuer through independently sourced contact; ask for proof the principal has the product; compare against other offers for the same lot.

entries.title: Counterparty due-diligence checklist
entries.in_plain_words: A standard set of checks for any new party.
entries.in_detail: Registry and good standing; directors and UBO; sanctions and adverse media screening; banking references verified directly; ISCC and other certificates verified in public databases; licences (MPOB, collection permits); audited accounts; trade references; site visit or video tour; email domain and phone verification; vessel and terminal checks.

entries.title: LC document-compliance check
entries.in_plain_words: Making sure documents match the credit before presenting.
entries.in_detail: Check each document against the LC line by line: goods description, quantities within tolerance, dates and presentation period, ports, Incoterm, B/L type and remarks, insurance, certificate wording, consistency of names and numbers, originals and copies required. Have the seller's bank pre-check drafts.

entries.title: Claims and disputes workflow
entries.in_plain_words: What to do when quality, quantity or payment is contested.
entries.in_detail: Give notice within the contract's time limit; preserve sealed samples; follow the contract's inspector and umpire procedure; negotiate; escalate to arbitration in the agreed seat; keep records. Delays can forfeit claims.

entries.title: Questions for a first meeting with a buyer
entries.in_plain_words: What to ask a plant or buyer before spending more time.
entries.in_detail: About them: end buyer or agent? who signs? plants and ISCC numbers? how they treat intermediaries? About the deal: exact feedstock and spec; certification and origin rules; cargo size and calendar; discharge ports, draft and terminal limits; preferred Incoterm; inspector; payment type, bank and timing; contract type and price formula; how and when commission is paid. About compliance: sanctions and origin policy; consequences of off-spec cargoes.

entries.title: Advance-fee schemes
entries.in_plain_words: Someone asks you or a party to pay money first to unlock a deal.
entries.in_detail: Fees for 'registration', 'inspection', 'proof of product', 'bank instrument', 'performance bond' or 'legal' before a verified contract. Legitimate firms rarely charge such fees to a counterparty before closing.
risks_and_red_flags: Fee requested before verified contract

entries.title: Bait pricing
entries.in_plain_words: A price far below the market to attract a buyer.
entries.in_detail: A big discount to published benchmarks, followed by demands for upfront fees. Compare with benchmarks from price-reporting agencies and any official reference prices.

entries.title: Fake proof of product
entries.in_plain_words: Pixelated PDFs, generic videos, Word-made receipts.
entries.in_detail: Check issuer, lot, tank and date. Verify with the terminal or lab directly. Refusal of independent verification is a strong red flag.

entries.title: Ghost vessels
entries.in_plain_words: A ship number that belongs to a vessel that is scrapped, elsewhere or does not exist.
entries.in_detail: Check IMO number, name history, AIS track, owner and manager in public ship databases and sanctions lists. Applies to FOB nominations as well as CIF.
entries.verify_note: Original said this only occurs in CIF sales.

entries.title: Shell beneficiaries and offshore routing
entries.in_plain_words: Payment to an opaque company or account unrelated to the seller.
entries.in_detail: Warning signs: beneficiary differs from the contracting party, last-minute change of beneficiary or bank, shell company in a secrecy jurisdiction. Triggers AML concerns.

entries.title: Fake escrow services
entries.in_plain_words: A newly created website that offers to hold the money.
entries.in_detail: Check regulation, years of operation, independent address and contact verification. Prefer a bank or a law firm client account you choose and verify.

entries.title: Domain spoofing and email impersonation
entries.in_plain_words: Emails that look like they come from a real company.
entries.in_detail: Look-alike domains, added hyphens or country codes, free mail accounts. Verify through contact details you find yourself and confirm payment changes by phone.

entries.title: The blind chain
entries.in_plain_words: Intermediaries who want an NCNDA but refuse video calls or registry documents.
entries.in_detail: No face, no verifiable company, no documents: stop. A chain that cannot show who stands at either end has no value.

entries.title: Circular trades
entries.in_plain_words: The cargo or paper returns to the start.
entries.in_detail: Company one sells to company two, company two sells to company three, and company three sells back to company one, with no real end buyer; often used to generate paper or financing. A string of principals on one cargo is legitimate when it ends with a real consumer; a circle is not. Related companies can hide the circle.

entries.title: Phantom principal
entries.in_plain_words: Someone presents as the seller but has no product.
entries.in_detail: Offers goods intending to buy them later. Detect by asking for title documents, upstream invoices and who signs the SPA.

entries.title: Mirror offers
entries.in_plain_words: The same lot offered through several routes at different prices.
entries.in_detail: Compare spec, volume, window, port and certificate numbers. If they match, it is one lot with several layers; the shortest and cheapest route is closest to the principal.

entries.title: Forged or altered documents
entries.in_plain_words: B/Ls, certificates, bank letters and inspection reports can be fake.
entries.in_detail: Verify with the issuer through independent contacts, check numbers in registries and databases, and watch for inconsistencies in dates, fonts, names and quantities.

entries.title: Virgin oil sold as used oil; multiple claiming
entries.in_plain_words: Fresh palm oil relabelled as UCO, or the same material certified twice.
entries.in_detail: Supply that exceeds plausible collection capacity, subsidised oil diverted to UCO channels, and double claims under mass balance are the typical patterns behind recent investigations.

entries.title: Fake or misused ISCC certificates
entries.in_plain_words: A certificate that does not exist, is expired or covers a different scope.
entries.in_detail: Verify certificate number, scope, site and validity in the public database; compare the legal name and address. Certification-body failures have led to sanctions.

entries.title: Fake LCs and MT799 'proof of funds'
entries.in_plain_words: A bank letter or message that looks real but creates no payment obligation.
entries.in_detail: A real LC arrives by SWIFT from the issuing bank to an advising bank. PDF 'LCs', MT799 messages sold by intermediaries and requests to pay a fee to receive one are red flags.

entries.title: Instrument 'monetization' and leasing schemes
entries.in_plain_words: Offers to buy, lease or monetize SBLCs and bank guarantees for a fee.
entries.in_detail: Legitimate banks issue instruments to their own clients under credit lines; instruments are not freely traded products. Lawful discounting of a real LC by a bank is different. Be wary of promised yields and upfront fees. A stated cost such as about 0.5% should be confirmed with the bank.

entries.title: Sanctions evasion patterns
entries.in_plain_words: Hiding who the real parties, ship or origin are.
entries.in_detail: Relabelled origin, intermediary shell companies, ship-to-ship transfers, AIS gaps, switching documents. Screen everything and keep records.

entries.title: Hidden related parties (the 'alter ego')
entries.in_plain_words: A second company under the same owners is used to bypass the broker.
entries.in_detail: Identify UBOs and affiliates; define parties in the NCNDA and commission agreement to include affiliates and successors.

entries.title: Fake or unknown inspectors and reports
entries.in_plain_words: An inspection company that does not exist or is not independent.
entries.in_detail: Check the firm's registration and accreditation, the inspector's contract role, and verify reports with the issuing office directly.

entries.title: Feedstock glossary: UCO, POME oil, PFAD and relatives
entries.in_plain_words: What each raw material is and how EU rules see it.
entries.in_detail: UCO (Annex IX Part B). POME oil (Annex IX Part A). EFB (Annex IX Part A). HAPOR: Indonesian term for high-acid palm oil residue. SPO: sludge palm oil, a low-grade mill residue; Malaysia classes used palm cooking oil as sludge. PFAD: refinery by-product, not in Annex IX and excluded from aviation fuel under ReFuelEU analyses. CPO: virgin crude palm oil, a food crop. Classification affects incentives and legality; verify per document.
options_and_variants: UCO: Used cooking oil
POME oil: Oil skimmed from palm oil mill effluent
EFB: Empty fruit bunches
HAPOR: High acid palm oil residue
SPO: Sludge palm oil
PFAD: Palm fatty acid distillate
CPO: Crude palm oil

entries.title: Price benchmarks
entries.in_plain_words: The published prices that deals are quoted against.
entries.in_detail: Price-reporting agencies such as Argus and Platts publish assessments; MPOB planned an official UCO reference price based on local delivered prices. Contracts name the exact benchmark and basis (FOB origin or CIF destination), the days used and premium or discount. Prices in this document are never examples to rely on.

entries.title: Price formulas
entries.in_plain_words: How a floating price is built.
entries.in_detail: Benchmark + premium or discount; pricing period; provisional invoice then final adjustment; currency and FX; quantity basis for the invoice.

entries.title: Where the money goes: cost stack, netback and your edge
entries.in_plain_words: Start from what the buyer will pay, subtract every cost, and see what the seller can realistically ask and where your fee fits.
entries.in_detail: Use the netback method. First take the buyer's target price: a named benchmark plus or minus a premium or discount, on a CIF or FOB basis. Then subtract, in order: ocean freight, cargo insurance (110% of value under CIF), inspection and sampling at load and discharge, terminal handling and heating, export clearance, inland transport to the port, pretreatment and quality adjustments, financing cost (LC fees plus interest for the days cash is tied up), certification premium, and every intermediary's commission. What is left is the most the seller can be paid at source. Compare it with the seller's real ask and with Malaysian local reference prices (MPOB planned an official UCO reference based on local delivered prices). An ask far below that netback points to bait pricing or hidden fraud; an ask far above means the buyer's price will not work. Every extra layer in the chain takes a fee from the same pool, so shorter chains leave room for a better price at both ends. Malaysia-specific levers: no export duty on UCO or POME oil as of an October 2025 report (duties were being considered); Indonesia's ban on crude POME and UCO exports pushes buyers toward other origins; MPOB licensing and monthly declarations give you documents to verify; and ports such as Port Klang and Pasir Gudang are the loading options to check for terminal capacity and heating. Your edge, to confirm and adjust: being physically in Kuala Lumpur lets you verify what most brokers only claim (site visits, terminal confirmations, direct contact with licensed collectors), which shortens chains and makes your introductions credible to European buyers. In the app, use the cost-stack calculator with your own quotes.
options_and_variants: Buyer target price: Benchmark plus or minus premium, with basis and pricing period
Ocean freight: Quote for the exact route, vessel size and date
Cargo insurance: 110% of cargo value under CIF
Inspection and sampling: Load port and discharge port
Terminal, heating and handling: Port and tank costs
Export clearance and inland transport: Customs, licences, trucking to port
Pretreatment and quality adjustment: Filtering, dehydration, penalties
Financing cost: LC fees plus interest for days of cash tied up
Certification premium: Cost of keeping the certified chain
Intermediary commissions: Every layer takes a share of the same pool
entries.verify_note: The 'edge' paragraph is an assumption about your position; adjust it. Cost figures must come from real quotes.

scenarios.title: The intermediary who wants an NCNDA but no video call
scenarios.situation: A contact offers 5,000 tonnes a month of UCO. He insists you sign his NCNDA first but refuses a video call and will not send registry documents.
scenarios.question: What do you do?
options: Sign the NCNDA to show good faith and ask for documents afterwards
Refuse to proceed until the company and its decision-makers can be verified
Pass the offer to your buyer and let the buyer check
Ask for a small fee-free sample first
scenarios.explanation: A chain that cannot show who stands at either end has no value. Signing first gives away your protection and your contacts, and passing it to the buyer risks your credibility.
what_to_do: Ask for registry extract, directors and beneficial owners
Insist on a video call with a decision-maker

scenarios.title: 5,000 tonnes a month from one supplier
scenarios.situation: A supplier claims it can ship 5,000 tonnes of UCO every month from Malaysia. It sends an ISCC certificate and a price well below the market benchmark.
scenarios.question: What is the first sensible check?
options: Accept the price because it is below market
Check the certificate in the public database and test whether the collection network could really generate that volume
Ask the buyer to prepay a deposit
scenarios.explanation: Collecting that volume from restaurants and food plants needs a very large network. A price far below benchmark, with volume beyond plausible capacity, is a classic sign of virgin oil being relabelled.
what_to_do: Verify certificate scope, sites and validity
Ask how many points of origin and which collectors
Ask for MPOB licence numbers and monthly declarations
Visit the site or have an independent party visit

scenarios.title: Four brokers between you and the seller
scenarios.situation: Your contact says the seller is 'behind three other brokers' but will pay everyone a share.
scenarios.question: What does this tell you?
options: It is normal and safe if everyone signs an NCNDA
Commissions will stack, nobody may have authority, and the price will probably not work
The seller must be very large
You should demand a higher share
scenarios.explanation: Each layer takes a fee from the same pool, and authority rarely reaches the owner. More than two undocumented layers is a stop.
what_to_do: Ask who the principal is and who signs the sales contract
Ask for the mandate documents of each layer
Try to reach the principal directly
Walk away if layers cannot be documented

scenarios.title: A sister company contacts your buyer
scenarios.situation: Weeks after you introduced a plant to a seller, a different company with the same address contacts the plant directly with a similar offer.
scenarios.question: What should your paperwork have covered?
options: Parties defined to include affiliates, successors and beneficial owners
scenarios.explanation: Defining the parties to include affiliates and beneficial owners closes the 'second company' route that is used to bypass brokers.
red_flags: Same address and owners, different name
what_to_do: Include affiliates in the NCNDA and commission agreement

scenarios.title: An ICPO that does not mention price
scenarios.situation: A buyer's ICPO lists product, volume, port and payment method but no price or discount.
scenarios.question: What do you do?
options: Start shopping it to sellers anyway
Ask for the price basis: benchmark, premium or discount, basis and pricing period
Ask the seller to propose the price
scenarios.explanation: Without a price basis you negotiate blind against the market. The buyer's target price gives you the ceiling and lets you test every offer.

scenarios.title: Proof of product that nobody can verify
scenarios.situation: A seller sends pixelated PDFs and a generic video. It refuses to let anyone contact the terminal or visit.
scenarios.question: How do you treat this?
options: As sufficient, because it sent documents
As a strong warning sign and ask for terminal confirmation or a visit
Ask the buyer to accept it
scenarios.explanation: Refusal of independent verification is a strong red flag. Copies prove nothing about existence, custody or title.
what_to_do: Ask the terminal to confirm in writing
Ask for upstream invoices and inspector reports
Arrange a visit or independent sampling

scenarios.title: Pay a fee to see a sample
scenarios.situation: A seller says a sample will be released after you pay a 'registration and handling' fee.
scenarios.question: What is this?
options: A normal cost of doing business
A sign of a premium supplier
scenarios.explanation: Fees for registration, proof, inspection or bonds before a verified contract are the advance-fee pattern.
what_to_do: Report if you were asked to introduce a buyer

scenarios.title: A large buyer will not sign your NCNDA
scenarios.situation: The buyer's compliance team says it never signs third-party NCNDAs but is happy to work with you.
scenarios.question: What is the best protection?
options: A direct commission agreement with the company, signed by an authorised signatory
Ask the seller to pay you more
scenarios.explanation: Large companies often refuse third-party NCNDAs. A commission agreement with the buyer itself is the most solid protection, and it should name affiliates and the payout trigger.
what_to_do: Ask who is authorised to sign
Define payer, trigger, route, duration and roll-overs

scenarios.title: English law or Spanish law?
scenarios.situation: The seller's draft says English law with London arbitration. The Spanish buyer wants Spanish law.
scenarios.question: What is the right way to think about it?
options: English law is mandatory in commodity trading
It is a choice: pick law and seat that both can accept, with an arbitration clause that is enforceable
scenarios.explanation: English law is common but not mandatory. Alternatives include Singapore, Malaysian or Spanish law with an agreed institution. Enforceability under the New York Convention matters.
what_to_do: Match the contract and the standard forms used

scenarios.title: A contract that says nothing about sustainability
scenarios.situation: The draft SPA covers price, quantity and delivery but is silent on certificates and proof of sustainability.
scenarios.question: What is missing?
options: Warranties about certification, a proof of sustainability with each cargo, mass balance duties and remedies if certificates fail
scenarios.explanation: The product is worth what the regulation lets it do. If the certificates fail, the buyer loses value, so the contract must make them a condition.

scenarios.title: Crude POME from Indonesia
scenarios.situation: A seller offers crude POME oil loading in Indonesia.
scenarios.question: What must you check first?
options: Whether crude POME and crude UCO exports are currently banned there and what grade is actually offered
scenarios.explanation: Indonesia has banned exports of crude POME and crude UCO since January 2025 (confirmed as maintained in February 2026). Refined grades were still exported. Always check the current rules.
what_to_do: Check the current rule and the product grade

scenarios.title: Escrow for a full cargo
scenarios.situation: A buyer proposes to pay a 5,000 tonne cargo through a law firm's escrow account.
scenarios.question: Why is this unusual?
options: It is the standard for bulk cargoes
Funds are locked while release depends on a third party, and a waiting ship runs up demurrage; letters of credit are the norm
scenarios.explanation: Escrow is rarely used for bulk cargoes. A confirmed LC or a standby-backed arrangement fits the physical timeline better.
what_to_do: Ask why not a letter of credit
Consider escrow only for small parcels

scenarios.title: Buy an SBLC from a provider
scenarios.situation: An intermediary says you can 'lease' or 'monetize' an SBLC for a fee to guarantee the deal.
scenarios.question: What is it?
options: A known scam pattern: banks issue instruments to their own clients, not as tradeable products
scenarios.explanation: Instruments are not freely traded products. Real bank discounting of a genuine LC is a different thing.
what_to_do: Verify any instrument bank to bank

scenarios.title: A letter of credit by email
scenarios.situation: A broker forwards a PDF 'LC' from the buyer's bank.
scenarios.question: How do you check?
options: Trust it because it has a logo
Have the seller's bank confirm it received the SWIFT message from the issuing bank
scenarios.explanation: A real LC is sent bank to bank by SWIFT. A PDF is not an LC.
what_to_do: Ask the seller's bank to verify the SWIFT message
Never act on the PDF alone

scenarios.title: The LC does not match the contract
scenarios.situation: The LC names a different discharge port and a quantity tolerance narrower than the SPA.
scenarios.question: What now?
options: Load anyway and fix it later
Ask the buyer to amend the LC before loading
Ask the bank to waive it
scenarios.explanation: After loading, mismatches cannot be repaired without risk. Amendments must be done before loading.

scenarios.title: The vessel that does not exist
scenarios.situation: The seller nominates a vessel whose IMO number belongs to a ship scrapped months ago.
scenarios.question: What do you do?
options: Treat it as a serious red flag and verify the vessel and its owners
scenarios.explanation: A ghost vessel is a known pattern. Verify the IMO number, history, owner and sanctions status in public databases.

scenarios.title: Two inspectors, two answers
scenarios.situation: The load-port inspector reports the cargo within spec; the buyer's laboratory says it is out of spec.
scenarios.question: What decides?
options: The contract: named inspector, final-and-binding rule, sealed samples and any umpire procedure
scenarios.explanation: Disputes are settled by the contract's procedure, using sealed samples and, if agreed, an umpire laboratory.

scenarios.title: The ship arrives before the original bill of lading
scenarios.situation: The vessel is at the discharge port but the original B/L is still travelling through banks.
scenarios.question: What is the safe route?
options: A letter of indemnity in the form agreed in the contract, normally backed by a bank
scenarios.explanation: The B/L is the title document. An indemnity lets the carrier release the cargo, but it should be pre-agreed and supported.
what_to_do: Get the indemnity countersigned by a bank

scenarios.title: A switch bill of lading
scenarios.situation: A trader proposes to replace the original B/L with a new one in its own name to hide the supplier.
scenarios.question: What is the issue?
options: It can obscure origin and traceability, which clashes with chain-of-custody rules, and is used in fraud
scenarios.explanation: Switch bills can break the traceability that certified sustainable material needs. Do not accept without understanding why.

scenarios.title: Relabel UCO as SPO to fit a licence
scenarios.situation: A Malaysian exporter suggests declaring UCO as sludge palm oil because its licence only covers SPO.
scenarios.question: What do you do?
options: Refuse and check what the product really is under current MPOB and customs rules
Ask the buyer to pay for a licence
scenarios.explanation: Declare exactly what the product is. Misdeclaring goods can lead to penalties and seizure and is the type of fraud authorities are now targeting.
what_to_do: Ask for MPOB licence and customs export licence
Do not proceed with a misdeclared cargo

scenarios.title: A buyer asks for EUDR guarantees
scenarios.situation: A European buyer asks for EUDR statements for a UCO cargo.
scenarios.question: What do you do?
options: Check whether the product is in scope or exempt waste or residue, and use the right application dates
scenarios.explanation: The EUDR applies from 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators, and scope for waste or residues depends on classification and the delegated act. Ask the buyer for its position.
what_to_do: Ask for the buyer's legal position

scenarios.title: The commission 'will be paid later'
scenarios.situation: The seller promises your fee after the deal but refuses to put payout terms in writing.
scenarios.question: What do you do?
options: Do not proceed without a written commission agreement with payer, trigger, route and roll-overs
Ask the buyer to pay instead
scenarios.explanation: Without a written payout trigger and route, your fee depends on goodwill. Banks do not pay it automatically from the SPA.
what_to_do: Define payer, trigger and wire route
Consider an assignment of proceeds if the bank agrees

glossary.definition: Certificate of analysis; also contract of affreightment
Delivered at place / unloaded / duty paid (Incoterms)
Federation of Oils, Seeds and Fats Associations
Letter of credit / documentary letter of credit
Letter of intent; also letter of indemnity (context decides)
SWIFT messages: documentary credit / guarantee or standby / free format
On board quantity / remaining on board

corrections_to_original.original_claim: The document contains 'all instruments' under ICC and UCP 600.
corrections_to_original.issue: It covers a fraction of the market, and mixes ICC-governed instruments with market-custom papers.
corrections_to_original.correction: Bible separates formal rules (UCP, URC, URDG, ISP98, Incoterms) from market customs (NCNDA, IMFPA, ICPO, SCO, FCO).

corrections_to_original.original_claim: T/T in advance must never be accepted or proposed.
corrections_to_original.issue: It is a legitimate method with trusted parties; high risk with unverified counterparties.
corrections_to_original.correction: Graded risk with safer variants (APG, escrow, payment against inspection).

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Soft PoP refusal of SGS pre-inspection means no product.
corrections_to_original.issue: Strong red flag but not proof; pre-inspection may be unavailable.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Ghost vessels happen in CIF sales.
corrections_to_original.issue: Also relevant to FOB nominations.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: At-sight LC pays in 3-5 days after presenting documents.
corrections_to_original.issue: UCP 600 gives banks up to five banking days to examine; payment follows compliant presentation.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Usance LC is paid 30/60/90 days after shipment.
corrections_to_original.issue: Maturity can run from B/L date, sight or acceptance; deferred payment and acceptance differ.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Transferable LC lets the trader keep margin without advancing money.
corrections_to_original.issue: Needs express 'transferable' wording, transferring bank and has limits (UCP 600 art. 38).

corrections_to_original.original_claim: CAD / D/P are the same; buyer's bank retains documents.
corrections_to_original.issue: D/P is a documentary collection under URC 522; CAD is a contract term; collecting bank handles documents.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: D/A is documents against a promissory note.
corrections_to_original.issue: It is against acceptance of a time draft (bill of exchange).

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Open account is commercial suicide.
corrections_to_original.issue: Normal between established parties, with insurance or standby protection.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Escrow is money blocked by a neutral bank or law firm.
corrections_to_original.issue: Correct in principle; agent must be regulated and verifiable; fake escrow is a known scam.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: SBLC is only for open-account trades.
corrections_to_original.issue: Also used as financial or performance guarantee; governed by ISP98 or UCP.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Performance bond is 2%-3%.
corrections_to_original.issue: No market-standard percentage; unsolicited bond-fee demands are a scam pattern.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: This is the exact chronological flow of deals.
corrections_to_original.issue: No universal order exists; buyer-led, seller-led and corporate flows differ.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Sanitised COA with lab and supplier names erased is acceptable proof.
corrections_to_original.issue: Unverifiable; acceptable only for a first screen.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Ask for a draft of a past PoS to validate GHG capability.
corrections_to_original.issue: A PoS is transaction-specific; ask for certificate number and verify in the ISCC database.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: ICPO is the foundational document and is sent before the NCNDA.
corrections_to_original.issue: An ICPO normally names the buyer, so it contradicts the rule to sign the NCNDA before disclosing identities.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: If a bank will not issue a BCL, a public corporate profile can replace it.
corrections_to_original.issue: A public profile does not prove ability to pay.
corrections_to_original.correction: Substitutes listed: audited accounts, credit report, verified credit line.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: NCNDA is an ICC contract.
corrections_to_original.issue: Not an ICC instrument; templates that cite ICC 400/500/600 reference LC rules.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: IMFPA becomes a bank payment order.
corrections_to_original.issue: It is a private contract; banks pay only on their instructions or LC terms.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: SCO is not legally binding.
corrections_to_original.issue: Usually intended as non-binding; wording and law decide.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: FCO is binding and lapses in 48-72 hours.
corrections_to_original.issue: Binding effect and validity period depend on wording and law.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: The seller's legal team normally drafts the SPA.
corrections_to_original.issue: Either party may; corporate buyers often use their own paper; sector forms exist.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Reference the IMFPA in the SPA so the bank processes the fee automatically.
corrections_to_original.issue: Banks do not process commissions from an SPA clause; naming broker fees may breach confidentiality.
corrections_to_original.correction: Separate agreement and payment instruction advised.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: English law and arbitration must always be used.
corrections_to_original.issue: Common, not mandatory; alternatives exist.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Laycan penalties are demurrage or deadfreight.
corrections_to_original.issue: Laycan is the loading window; demurrage compensates excess laytime; deadfreight is unused-space freight.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: SGS inspection is final and binding.
corrections_to_original.issue: The contract names the inspector; final-and-binding has carve-outs.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: B/L must say CLEAN ON BOARD.
corrections_to_original.issue: 'Shipped on board' and 'clean' are separate attributes; switch B/Ls can obscure traceability.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Q&Q certificate is the official verdict.
corrections_to_original.issue: Independent inspector's certificates, not governmental; quality and quantity are separate.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Invoice equals SGS tons times average Argus price.
corrections_to_original.issue: Price mechanics are set in the SPA and invoices may be provisional and final.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: PoS is registered in the UDB.
corrections_to_original.issue: PoS is issued under the certification scheme; operators record transactions in the UDB as required.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: MPOB export licence proves payment of FOB tariffs.
corrections_to_original.issue: FOB is an Incoterm, not a duty; MPOB licences relate to palm-industry activities; export clearance goes through customs; no export duty on UCO/POME oil as of Oct 2025 but under consideration.
corrections_to_original.correction: Malaysia entries added with verification date.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Insurance under CIF must be Institute Cargo Clauses A.
corrections_to_original.issue: Minimum cover under Incoterms 2020 CIF is (C); CIP requires (A).

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Missing items.
corrections_to_original.issue: Document omitted many instruments, rules, documents, regulations and risks.
corrections_to_original.correction: Bible adds back-to-back and revolving LCs, confirmation, assignment, guarantees, URC/URDG/ISP98, RED II/III, Annex IX, ISCC roles, EUDR, Indonesia ban, Malaysia rules, compliance and more.

corrections_to_original.original_claim: Absolute statements ('never', 'always').
corrections_to_original.issue: Overstates certainty and teaches bad habits.

changelog.change: Removed every table-style label (V1, C4, P-B-P and similar) from the role and chain entries. The chain catalogue and the roles entry are now written in natural language.

Kept 30 December 2026 (large and medium operators and traders) and 30 June 2027 (micro and small operators). Checked on 18 Oct 2026: the December 2025 amendment fixed these dates, the Commission's May 2026 review said no further delay or reopening is planned, and sources from the last days still use 30 December 2026. An end-of-2027 date appears only for products newly added to Annex I. If a buyer cites another date, ask for the source.

Replaced the theoretical text with the netback method, Malaysia-specific levers, a cost-line checklist and an explicit paragraph on your edge as a broker based in Kuala Lumpur (marked as an assumption to adjust). The app now includes a cost-stack calculator.

Confidence lowered to medium and the entry now says that escrow is not a bulk-cargo standard: locked funds, release depending on third parties and demurrage risk. It fits small parcels, deposits or performance deposits. Added a scenario.
The ICPO entry now requires a target price or formula: named benchmark, premium or discount, FOB or CIF basis and pricing period. Added a scenario and a stage gate.

Rewrote the MPOB entry. Verified: used palm cooking oil is classified as sludge palm oil under the MPOB (Licensing) Regulations 2005, four activities are licensed, exporting CPO, processed palm oil and SPO needs a customs export licence under the Customs (Prohibition on Exports) Order 2017, and MPOB has been reviewing how to separate UCO from SPO. Added the rule never to relabel a product to fit a licence. Not verified: immediate seizure on the K2 declaration and different duties for SPO and UCO; these are flagged for a customs lawyer.
